speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: STATEMENT AS TO PLANE PROVIDED FOR TRIP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Prince Albert made an inquiry yesterday about the aircraft used by His Excellency the Governor General on his recent flight from Ottawa to Calgary as part of his western tour. I agreed with him that Her Majesty's representative should always have the best means of transportation available for any of his official tours. The Ottawa Journal said yesterday:
When Prime Minister St. Laurent checks into the reason why the government's far-travelled luxury aircraft, the C-5, wasn't available to take the Governor General west, he will find that he himself was responsible.
That is probably true. I was on the C-5 returning to Ottawa on July 7 and reached Ottawa about 45 minutes after His Excellency had taken off for Calgary in the North Star aircraft No. 17520, which he had used for his northern trip. I can assure the house that when it was decided it would be preferable for me to travel to and from London by air for the prime ministers' conference in London so as to be away from the house as short a time as possible, I was somewhat disappointed because I had hoped earlier that it would be possible for me to travel by sea.
I was quite unaware that making the C-5 available to take me to and from London would interfere in any way with any plan for a flight on an official tour that His Excellency might wish to make. I was informed that when inquiry was made whether the C-5 would be available my office was informed that it would be available, that before giving that answer there had been communications with His Excellency's secretary, and that His Excellency had expressed the desire that the C-5, which is the only government plane that is proper for a transAtlantic flight, be used for that flight. Had I known that it was going to interfere with any plan that had been made for His Excellency's own flights on an official tour in
Canada I certainly would have insisted that other arrangements be made, because I think these tours of His Excellency as Her Majesty's representative are extremely important.
It had been suggested to His Excellency that the Viscount, which is the only other pressurized plane in the government service, be placed at His Excellency's disposal. But His Excellency felt-and quite properly, in my opinion- that because there was going to be a guard of honour to receive him at Calgary it would be preferable for him to arrive there in an R.C.A.F. plane rather than in a plane in the service of the Department of Transport. But it certainly would have been possible for me and my department to make other arrangements and I would have insisted that they be made. I know it is difficult to secure accommodation on commercial lines without long notice with regard to reservations, but I am sure it would have been possible to have those arrangements made. I certainly would have endeavoured to avoid a situation, though I was unconscious of it, which would allow any newspaper to say that I myself was responsible for the fact that this plane which His Excellency had used for his northern flight-and which was the only one that was appropriate for the flight and which he had found very comfortable-would be used for this flight to Calgary.
I am sorry the incident occurred, because I quite agree with the hon. gentleman and I feel that hon. members of the house will agree that these official tours are an extremely useful part of the way His Excellency is carrying out his duties and responsibilities as Her Majesty's representative in Canada.

speechtext: should like to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: CANADIAN VIEW OF RUSSIA'S SUGGESTION TO END EXPERIMENTATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we are studying with great interest the speech given yesterday by the Soviet foreign minister which dealt with this matter, but have not yet come to any conclusions with regard to it. As my hon. friend knows, the disarmament commission has been meeting in New York. It concluded its meetings last evening. At this session my friend and colleague the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) made a statement on Canada's policy in this matter. Whether as a result of the statement made in Moscow yesterday by the Soviet foreign minister our position should be revised in any way is a matter we are now considering.

maintopic: CANADIAN VIEW OF RUSSIA'S SUGGESTION TO END EXPERIMENTATION
speechtext:
May I ask the minister
whether the representative of Canada at the United Nations recently stated the attitude of Canada toward the Krishna Menon proposals before the disarmament commission? Did Canada make a statement at that time, and if so what was our position?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: CANADIAN VIEW OF RUSSIA'S SUGGESTION TO END EXPERIMENTATION
speechtext:
My colleague the
Secretary of State for External Affairs has suggested that I might supplement what he has said in answer to the question just now put. Canada was one of the two nations that suggested Mr. Menon should be allowed, although not a member of the disarmament commission, to make representations on behalf of his government with regard to the question of the banning of nuclear tests. Canada was the country that yesterday suggested that when the subcommittee of the disarmament commission resumes its sittings at a date not yet decided, special note should be taken of the representations made by the delegate for India.
Canada has taken the position in the disarmament commission that it was in favour of the cessation of nuclear tests when this

cessation could take place at a time, and under conditions, that would not prejudice the security of the nations concerned. We did indicate our sympathetic interest in the suggestion that a committee of experts might be designated to consider a limitation on the number and nature of test explosions. We asserted that we would give consideration as well to the banning of explosions for military purposes, to be closely coupled with a controlled ban on manufacturing for military purposes. But it must be clear that if there was not agreement on this subject it was not because of any action taken by any western nation. This ban could take place if the Soviet union would agree to the kind of controls which are desirable and necessary in this situation.

maintopic: CANADIAN VIEW OF RUSSIA'S SUGGESTION TO END EXPERIMENTATION
speechtext: May I ask a further question. Do I understand that Canada does not require that this shall be a part of a general disarmament agreement? Is that right?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: CANADIAN VIEW OF RUSSIA'S SUGGESTION TO END EXPERIMENTATION
speechtext: Canada's statement was that we would agree to such a cessation in the context of an agreement on disarmament. This does not mean that there must be a comprehensive state of disarmament. We would agree to such cessation, within the context of an agreement on disarmament, effective at an appropriate stage and under conditions that would assure our security.

subsubtopic: REFUSAL TO ISSUE REVOLVER LICENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am now in position to make a statement with regard to a matter which was raised yesterday by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) and the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), and which was raised with me some weeks ago by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Applewhaite), concerning the issuing of permits to trappers and prospectors in the northern area of British Columbia to enable them to carry pistols and revolvers in connection with their work.
Section 90 of the Criminal Code makes it an offence for a person to have a pistol or revolver elsewhere than in his dwelling house or place of business unless he has a valid permit. Section 94 of the code authorizes the commissioner of the mounted police and the attorney general of the province to issue such permits. Since section 94 places the authority for the issuance of permits within the province in the hands of the attorney general of the province, the commissioner of the mounted police confines his authority to issuing permits to those of an interprovincial nature, such as permits to express messengers.
In those provinces such as British Columbia, in which the government of Canada has entered into an agreement with the provincial government to make available the services of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to discharge provincial police duties, it is the

Inquiries of the Ministry provincial attorney general who controls the policy under which those authorized to issue permits, including officers of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, must issue them. Moreover, the officers of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, in the issuance of permits for pistols and revolvers in such a province, are, pursuant to the police agreement, under the direction of the provincial attorney general. I suggest, therefore, that my hon. friend's question might be more appropriately directed to the attorney general of British Columbia.

subsubtopic: REFUSAL TO ISSUE REVOLVER LICENCES
speechtext: I have a submission from the British Colum-bia-Yukon chamber of mines on this question which I should like to place before the Minister of Justice. In view of the fact that these men were permitted to carry revolvers for many years up until this year, will he not make some effort to see that they are allowed to have revolvers this year, even though it means making representations to the provincial government?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REFUSAL TO ISSUE REVOLVER LICENCES
speechtext: I have no hesitation in agreeing to do anything that is reasonably within my power in that connection; but I must say that where we have a police agreement between a province and the dominion we do make a special effort not to appear to take advantage of that fact to impose anything more than suggestions upon the provincial attorney general in respect to matters which fall within the jurisdiction of the province. It would really be much more appropriate, if I may say so, if my hon. friend would raise this matter with the Hon. Mr. Bonner, whose responsibility it is, and have him do it. I do not like, as a co-signer with Mr. Bonner of the British Columbia police agreement, to be suggesting to him how he should handle his end of that.

subsubtopic: REFUSAL TO ISSUE REVOLVER LICENCES
speechtext: Is it not a fact that the basic trouble is the terms of the Criminal Code itself, and that that is a matter for amendment here?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REFUSAL TO ISSUE REVOLVER LICENCES
speechtext: No, not at all. I think there would be general agreement in the house that so far as the discretion in the issuance of permits of this sort is concerned, it can be far more appropriately exercised by the provincial or local authorities than by myself or my officials in Ottawa. It would not be reasonable that a man in northern British Columbia wanting to carry a revolver should have to write to the Minister of Justice; and if he did, what would we know about the circumstances under which he was going to carry it?

subsubtopic: REFUSAL TO ISSUE REVOLVER LICENCES
speechtext: Why should the code not permit the carrying of a revolver by this type of person?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REFUSAL TO ISSUE REVOLVER LICENCES
speechtext: For reasons that were gone into at length at the time this particular section was debated, i do not want to review them now, but I would point out to my hon. friend that if we did not have a restriction of this kind on the carrying of revolvers by people circulating around the country, everybody could carry them, with consequences that I feel he might deplore.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when I began last night I suggested that an appropriate test by which this resolution might be judged was whether or not it tended to maintain the federal system or even to reduce the overcentralization which has been a continuing legacy of the war. I suggested that there was one bright ray appearing, in that the new arrangement seems to leave in an equal position a province which wishes to rent its tax fields and a province which wishes to collect its own taxes, in other words to share its foimer tax fields with the federal government, and that the proposal would be equally beneficial, if you want to put it that way or would be equally harmful, if you want to put it the other way.
The minister's assessment of the provincial attitude toward his proposals is contained in his remark that not one province over a period of 15 months, I think he said, had said that the new plan was not as good as the tax rental agreements. It strikes me that is pretty faint praising by the minister of his own proposal and of the provincial reaction to it. It seems clear to me that the provinces have not reacted favourably to the new proposals. They have recognized an advance, as we do, in the respect which I have mentioned. They have also recognized that there is more money for them. I think the minister estimates that there is 20 per cent more money.
It is perhaps significant to note that the corresponding grants from the province of Ontario to its municipalities have increased in the last five years by something like 190 per cent. I think that is approximately the figure, but I will get the exact figure. In any event there is a 20 per cent increase under the resolution and bill, and that is not to be overlooked. But notwithstanding the two things that can be said and which I have said, it seems clear that the provinces are dissatisfied. They have spoken for themselves, and it is not necessary for us to speak for them today. But I think it is desirable that this committee should have the provincial viewpoint expressed very clearly, because to my

They have been going in the direction of centralization of authority in Ottawa. Seventeen years is a long time, long enough for most ministers to form habits!
There is no question but that the government enjoys the position it holds in confederation. The members of the government have even, I think, attributed to themselves a certain indispensability which is not calculated to improve relationships between the central and the provincial governments. If I may say so, they have the attitude that no one can do it like we do, that we are the best spenders Canada has ever had. There is no question but that they are the biggest and the fastest spenders.
Mr. Chairman, it began with the Rowell-Sirms commission report. That report planted the seed of an idea. It did more than plant it; it expounded a theory that full employment could be maintained in Canada if the great progressive taxes, namely the income tax and the corporation tax, were centralized m the hands of Ottawa. I think that report could not have been more satisfactory to Mr. King if he himself had written it. In any event he seemed to accept, as have his successors, the central theme that if we are' to have no more unemployment-and all governments have made that one of their objectives-the more centralization control of the economy there is in Ottawa, the better it is for everybody.
That is the thesis I want to challenge. That is where it began. The provinces would have none of it. However, the war came to the rescue of the government and under the real and grave necessities of the war and the essential need for a unified command, we had a centralized authority and centralized tax collection, and all the provinces entered into agreements

Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements which handed over completely to the federal government their right to levy personal incomes taxes and corporation income taxes. That was a complete vacation of a field which the provinces enjoyed under the constitution equally with the federal government. They were joint tenants, if I may put it that way; and my conception of a joint tenancy is one in which each party has a fifty-fifty interest, in the absence of other arrangements.
That was the position. They had equal rights in that field, and I do not believe anybody would deny that as a constitutional and legal concept. In any event, the provinces, with very strong assurances that they would be restored to their former rights, gave up completely their taxing authority in those two fields for the duration of the war.
Then after the war, in the 1945 and 1946 dominion-provincial conferences, called the reconstruction conferences, the provinces were presented with the green book which was an ambitious scheme to continue the effect and carry on the general ideas of the Rowell-Sirois commission's report and to continue the centralized authority over and control of the economy which was the basis of that recommendation. At that conference the provinces were anxious to agree, but they were unconvinced and they were divided, and in the end they were forced to accept.
The next event was the budget of Mr. llsley, brought down in 1946, which to some [DOT]extent resembles the proposals under which we still are obliged to work, an arrangement by which those who were unconvinced, and unwilling to leave their birthright in the hands of the federal government, would be obliged to continue on their own, with such abatement and recognition as Ottawa chose to give. Quebec and Ontario undertook to maintain their independence and go their own way and for the next few years they levied corporation taxes at the rate of 7 per cent, although the federal government's allowance to their taxpayers was only 5 per cent. They did not levy personal income taxes; that field was left entirely to the federal government.
Then in 1950 there was a further conference. The first agreement had been a three-year agreement and obviously was only a stop-gap agreement pending some more comprehensive solutions of these matters. In 1950 there was a conference in the shadow of the Korean conflict, and as a result of that conference new agreements were made in 1952. At that time Ontario joined in the agreement to rent these tax fields for a period of five years, leaving Quebec as the only province which remained outside the agreement; and until this day Quebec has stoutly maintained its independent position.
[Mr. Michener.l
I think those who believe that the federal system means something in this country and should be preserved owe a great deal to the fortitude of the people of Quebec, who have maintained that position throughout the last ten years since the war. But even Quebec felt the pinch of the conditions with which they were confronted, and in 1954 and 1955 met something of a crisis which required the province to levy income taxes of their own, something which proved to be an embarrassment to them, and certainly to the federal government, and which resulted in a concession from Ottawa, namely a 10 per cent abatement in the personal income tax field.
I think that is probably the genesis of the new agreements or the new arrangements which are now under consideration.
These agreements which were made in 1952 run out in 1957. The opportunities to provide a more satisfactory and comprehensive arrangement to meet present day needs are also running out. No solution has been found. The minister has propounded a principle to which I subscribe, namely that the provinces' revenues should be consistent with their responsibilities, but that result has not been achieved. The revenues which the provinces might enjoy have been rented under the circumstances I have recounted. They have been withheld; some say they have been filched away from them by the overweening central authority which does not wish to return those taxing powers to the provinces.
I suggest that the position today can be readily appreciated by looking at a table showing a comparison of the spending by the federal government and by the provincial and municipal governments over the last few years and by seeing how the balance has shifted toward the central authority. I am quoting from table 7 in the Canadian Tax Foundation's review entitled "The National Finances", 1955-56. It appears at page 12. The comparison is between the expenditures, which I think is the true basis rather than the revenues. The revenues are even more in favour of the federal government, but they do not take into account intergovernmental payments.
The expenditures in 1929 by the central government were $323 million and by the provincial and municipal governments, $600 million. I see that the minister has the table before him. To express it in percentages, the federal government was spending 5-2 per cent of the gross national product and the provincial and municipal governments were spending 9-7 per cent or almost twice what the federal government was spending. In 1933 the provincial and municipal governments spent 16-5 per cent of the gross

national product as against 8 [DOT] 5 per cent spent by the Ottawa government. Those were depression times, and the weight of the depression on the municipalities was extremely heavy. In 1945-and this is the next comparison I should like to make-we find that a complete reversal had taken place. In that year we find that the central government was spending 34-6 per cent or more than one-third of the gross national product, and the provincial and municipal governments were down to 6-8 per cent, a smaller proportion than they had spent at any time previously.
We now come up to date. In 1954, which is the last year for which figures are given, the amount spent by the federal government was $4,142 million and that was 17-2 per cent of the gross national product; the provinces and municipalities combined spent $2,447 million, which was only 10-2 per cent of the gross national product. If one quoted the figures for collections for the same year one would find that in 1954 the federal government collected 19 per cent of the gross national product and that the provinces and municipalities combined collected 8-5 per cent.
That is a complete reversal in the short period of one generation and all of it has taken place under the aegis of this government. It is for that reason I say the provinces have little to hope for from a government that has that record and that background. They have been conditioned, as the psychologists say, to the belief that the welfare of Canadians stems from what is done in Ottawa rather than what is done by local governments.
I have been speaking about revenues, and now let me say one word about the responsibilities of different levels of government. There has been no determined effort to resettle their responsibilities, either in line with this sharing of revenues and expenditures or on any settled principle. Here again there has been an encroachment by the federal authority, partly I suppose because it has had the funds with which to meet the needs. The provincial governments, as I say, have been occupying a lesser position throughout. This point was well expressed by Mr. Hicks, the premier of Nova Scotia, when he spoke to the Canadian club in Toronto on January 25 of last year. He said that without the people knowing it or deciding it, the basis of the constitutional relationship was being changed and that the federal government was encroaching in almost all fields, agriculture, fisheries, transport, finance, education, labour, health, pensions, highways; all those provincial fields had been encroached upon by the federal government.

Every one of them has been done, as Mr. Hicks indicated, without any arrangement. This has resulted, no doubt, because the resources were available to the central government. That is demonstrated by the fact that the clamour for money is directed to Ottawa, and for many things which are purely provincial in their concern. This is particularly true of education and highways. There is a path worn to the minister's doorstep in connection with all these matters, which are matters of provincial concern. The reason is that Ottawa has money to burn. I do not know what the minister's surplus will be this year, but I suggest to him it may run as much as $750 million. I hope it will. With a surplus of the kind which he will have to present, if he is not able to conceal it. he is not going to be very popular with the provincial finance ministers in endeavouring to settle their problems on the basis he is proposing to this house today.
What is needed, Mr. Chairman, is a new look, because the war has been over for some years and the cold war, while it is making constant demands, is taking a secondary place to the industrial growth and peacetime development of this economy. I suggest that our expanding economy is soundly based on the possession of resources that the world needs, and that the main problem is to create a condition in which those resources can be used and developed. Wealth, Mr. Chairman, is not created at Ottawa. It comes not from Ottawa, but from the ground and from the work of the people of this country. Ottawa has failed, I suggest, to see that there is a change; that what was desirable 15 years ago and what was represented by the Rowell-Sirois commission is no longer appropriate to meet the needs of the time.
The truth of this assertion can be readily demonstrated by the condition of the municipalities and provinces and the services they have to perform. This expansion of our economy rests on the services which are provided locally. It rests on a grass roots development throughout every part of Canada. The municipalities are struggling with a problem which they are unable to meet. I should like to cite one or two examples to demonstrate to the house how, in a few short years, the responsibilities of the municipalities have changed. The city of Kitchener is a typical example of an expanding city. Its total debenture debt in 1951 was $6-8 million. By 1954 it was over $10-25 million. Its school debt in 1951 was $1,169,000. In 1954, it was $2 million.
This rate of increase in the school debt amounted to 77-3 per cent in four short years, and that is not unusual. There is one municipality in the province, Dundas, where
6058	HOUSE OF
Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements school debt increased by 813 per cent in the same period. Throughout the whole of Ontario the municipalities-and they are the ones I naturally would use to illustrate this point-were faced with an enormous increase in their responsibilities, an increase in debt and in the levy of taxes for schools and other municipal services. In Toronto the increase in the school debenture debt in that same period was 165 per cent.
Now let me further illustrate by levies in some of these centres. The tax levy in Kitchener increased from 1951 to 1954, for all purposes by 55 per cent and for school purposes by 57 per cent. In a smaller community like the township of Toronto, where there is a great deal of activity resulting from the industrial development in the Toronto area, the total tax levy increased from 1951 to 1954 by 121 per cent and the total school levy by 165 per cent. Those are only figures, but what do they mean to the ordinary person who lives in the township of Toronto and pays his taxes there? They are a staggering burden for the home owner, and it cannot be tolerated for long. Yet there is no visible end to this problem short of some general readjustment which will give the provinces greater financial resources.
There is one other illustration.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman.
The provincial problem is of the same order. I should say that these levies made by the municipalities for school purposes are made after the provincial grants to the municipalities which this year in Ontario for all purposes, including education, are $184 million or 40 per cent of the total Ontario provincial budget. If one can imagine such a transfer of funds, that is what is taking place. Ontario's total budget of over $400 million has to be paid over, to the extent of 40 per cent, to the municipalities.
The provinces have their own part to play in maintaining our prosperity. This results mainly from their control and direction of our natural resources. The provinces must plant, but Ottawa reaps the harvest. This situation cannot go on. I should like, Mr. Chairman, to use the figures for Ontario


forests and mines to show exactly how the federal government benefits from the developments which are mainly made at the expense of the provincial governments. In the forestry department the Ontario government revenues, made up of timber dues, fire tax and other department of lands and forests receipts, totalled $20 million. The treasury department receives a logging tax of $800,000, making total revenues to the province of Ontario from these lands and forests of $20,800,000. The total federal tax declared by Ontario's forest-based industries was $39-3 million, that is just about twice what the province received from industries working in this natural resource and which depend on the province and municipalities for services that sustain those industries, and without which they could not operate. Yet Ottawa, as I say, reaped a harvest of approximately $40 million, twice as much as the province, in the same field.
In mining the contrast is even more striking. If the government were at all receptive to the importance of the activities of the municipalities and the provinces in these fields they would appreciate that this condition cannot continue. From mining the Ontario government receives a total of $5-2 million, whereas the total federal tax taken from the Ontario mining industry is $27-4 million, or more than five times the amount which the provincial government receives in taxes from its mining industry.
This situation can be very simply illustrated by the kind of development we see going on everywhere in Canada. At Bancroft, in Ontario, one of the uranium mines is making an expenditure of $10 million in a mill and mining plant. That involves the province in the construction of roads; it involves the municipalities in building schools to house the children of a community of 5,000 people, and all the incidental services that are necessary to establish a community without which a mine cannot function. These miners begin to pay taxes to the federal government from their very first pay cheques; while the mill is in the process of building, the federal government draws excise and sales taxes and that sort of revenue, and as soon as the plant begins to operate the profit tax begins to roll into Ottawa.
Up to the present time the federal government has not expended one cent in the ground work which makes the industry possible. It is true they have, under their direction, arranged for the sale of uranium, which they control. To that extent they have a part, but there has been no cost to the federal government. The cost of all of this is on the

municipality and the province, and the disproportion of the resulting revenues for government purposes is five to one in favour of the federal government. Now, Mr. Chairman, that is a condition that I say cannot continue. The clamour at the door of Ottawa is the proof that there is an imbalance which is of serious proportions. A broader conference is needed, Mr. Chairman, and a resettlement of the responsibilities and revenues.
The minister has said that time and men both change and our problems change with them. There is no hope of a broad federal solution from this government, with the background I have illustrated. Change is taking place, and a change in the approach to these problems is needed. If the government will not change, Mr. Chairman, I suggest it is time to change the government.
I wish to close, Mr. Chairman, with one more quotation from a man who was quoted with considerable relish by the other side of the house not so long ago. Mr. Frost, the premier of Ontario, in speaking about these negotiations in the Ontario legislature on March 12, 1956, said, as reported at page 929 of the Ontario Hansard:
I tell this house today that the federal government has deplorably failed to assess the needs of the provinces and their municipalities which are the right arm of peacetime development and expansion. They are as wrong In this as they were in the attitude of 1945 and 1950. The unfortunate part is that this matter is urgent, that our taxpayers are being overwhelmed because they are being deprived of their fair share of the revenues which come from the very production which causes our problems. That the federal government will be proved wrong again I have no doubt, but it is my hope that it will not be too late, before they find they are wrong, unfair and unjust to the provinces.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to speak briefly in this debate. I do so because of some of the comments that were made yesterday afternoon and evening. I should like to make particular reference to the maritime provinces, and particularly again to the province of Nova Scotia of which I am one of the representatives.
Statements were made yesterday that the maritime provinces in general are being treated unfairly by the federal government; that the federal government was doing nothing, or at least was not doing nearly enough, to assist in the economy of the maritime provinces; that there was a lack of defence expenditures in the maritime provinces; that the present proposed tax rentals, including the tax equalization payments, were not large enough, and so on. In doing so, one or two of the speakers made slight reference to other expenditures which are made by the federal government, and I do feel that if
17, 1956	6059
Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements one is going to look at the proposal as set out in this resolution, one must in fairness look at other expenditures being made by the federal government.
I should like to speak briefly of three of our main industries in Nova Scotia, our three primary industries, mining, fishing and agriculture. I do not think it is generally realized by Nova Scotians, and I am sure it is not by many members in this house, that in so far as the mining of coal, for example, in Nova Scotia is concerned, five federal government assistance grants are received. I am sure that no one has any idea, or very few have any idea, of the magnitude of those grants. For example, from the transportation subvention, which is to overcome to some extent the handicap of the distance of the coal mines from the main markets in the central provinces of Ontario and Quebec, in 1954-55, the last year for which final figures are available, the province of Nova Scotia received $8,689,000. Since this subvention assistance was put into effect in 1929 the province of Nova Scotia has received over $55,600,000.
Another form of assistance is the subsidy payments on coal which is used in the manufacture of iron and steel. This goes back to the coke bounty act of 1930. Under this act and under the Canadian Coal Equality Act of 1952 Nova Scotia, in 1954-55, received $224,600. Since that act has been in effect, from 1931, Nova Scotia has received almost exactly $7 million.
The third form of assistance for the coal industry is the coal production subsidies, the loans and the rentals. Under this plan there are long-term loans made for the purpose of increasing efficiency of production through modernized mechanization. Nova Scotia has received under this plan over $30 million; to be exact, $30,863,000 over a period of five years.
Then there is the coal production assistance loan under which we have received in the last six years $7,600,000 and, of course, the export subsidy on coal which brought us in the last year $300,000. I mention these, Mr. Chairman, just to show that in coal alone, not only recently but over the last few years, Nova Scotia has received very large sums to assist its mining industry.
We do hear a little more in the house about the freight assistance under the Maritime Freight Rates Act, which provides a reduction of 20 per cent on all freights charged on certain traffic originating and terminating within certain designated areas. Unfortunately, at the moment I have not the exact figure for the last year for Nova Scotia, but the maritime provinces and the Atlantic

Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements provinces were referred to yesterday. In the Atlantic region the freight assistance amounted to $10,590,000 in 1954-55, and within the last nine years it has amounted to over $77,500,000.
In so far as fisheries are concerned, there are many avenues in which the federal government is assisting the fisheries in the maritime provinces. For example, there is the fishing bounty which is to aid in the development of the sea fisheries of Canada. In 1954-55 Nova Scotia received approximately $85,000, and within the last 10 years $839,300. There is assistance in the form of educational service for fishermen, which is to extend the educational work in co-operative producing and selling among fishermen. The maritimes received last year, under this item $46,000, and in the last 10 years the maritimes received in round figures $460,000. There is also assistance in the form of industrial development to provide for expenditures in so far as technical service to fishermen is concerned, and in that regard the maritimes in 1954-55 received nearly $250,000 and in the last three years received about $370,000.
There is construction assistance for fishing vessels, which is of great value particularly in my own province of Nova Scotia in so far as the construction of draggers and the long liner type of vessels are concerned. In this case the subsidy payments are made through the fishery loan agencies, and in the maritimes they amounted to almost exactly $114,000 during the year 1954-55 and during the last eight years have amounted to approximately $658,000.
Still another form of assistance is that given to bait freezers. That is of particular interest to my own constituency, where several have already been built and others are under construction. In the last seven years that has amounted to $65,000 for Nova Scotia and a large part of that has gone into the constituency of Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare.
In so far as agriculture is concerned I think one of the best moves made in recent years was the passing of the Maritime Marshland Reclamation Act. Under this act Nova Scotia received $733,000 in 1954-55, and in the last seven years it received nearly $2J million. That program has gradually been developed, and each year the expenditures increase and doubtless will continue to increase for a few years until the program is still further developed. This program provides for the construction of dikes and aboiteaux to reclaim the marshlands. This is a co-operative arrangement between the federal and provincial governments and the marshland owners.


There is another form of assistance which goes to maritime farmers, namely the agricultural lime assistance program. Under this program in the last nine years Nova Scotia has received over $500,000.
In addition to the freight assistance I mentioned earlier, which applies to all traffic moving in certain designated areas, there is freight assistance on western feed grains which represents a considerable amount and makes a vast difference in the economy of the farming areas of Nova Scotia. In 1954-55 Nova Scotia received $1,600,000 under this form of assistance, and has received in the last nine years over $13 million.
One could go on in great detail, Mr. Chairman, and one could quote a great many figures, but I think I have perhaps given enough figures concerning mining, fishing and agriculture to show that there are a great many forms of assistance and a number of ways in which the maritime provinces in general and Nova Scotia in particular receive funds from the federal government in addition to the proposal we have in this resolution today.
To give another example, there are the general health grants under the Department of National Health and Welfare. In 1954-55 in Nova Scotia these amounted to $2J million, and over the last seven years since they were inaugurated they have amounted to over $8J million.
So much for the general forms of assistance. In Nova Scotia we have also had a great many individual development projects over the last few years, many of which have been discussed in the house. I think it might perhaps be just as well to mention four or five of them. For example, there was the development of the North Sydney terminals, which in the last few years amounted to approximately $3J million. In the last ten years the expenditures of the national harbours board amounted to over $6,300,000. The general vote for harbours and rivers varies from year to year, but in 1954-55 it was over $3 million in Nova Scotia.

I noticed that yesterday the minister was a little plaintive when referring to the short time which had been given to the resolution in 1952. I looked that up and found that only about an hour and a half had been spent discussing it. The minister should not complain because in 1952 our war troubles were still alarming and the tax agreements were just a continuation of those of 1947. The major advance in Canadian life had just begun four years ago, and the tax rental agreements of that time were carried on without too prolonged a discussion.
But the situation has changed materially. We have reached a stage where the pressures or fears of a world war have diminished. They are still present to a certain extent but they have diminished, because the possible destruction resulting from a thermonuclear war has alarmed even the most aggressive of nations. Although we have to make preparation for war in the future, the fact is that we are not in the same state of despondency regarding the world as we have been for the last few years. That has eased the pressure to a certain extent and has given us a chance to look at other matters within the state. Hence the more prolonged discussion at this time with regard to dominion-provincial tax arrangements.
I think that is the sensible way to look at this matter, because we are now on the threshold of great advances in Canada and there is no reason why we cannot look forward to a period of peace, a reduction in armaments and a general easing of tension. Under those circumstances the reasons which kept the wartime tax rental agreements in

operation in Canada must be considered as having ceased to exist, and a new look should be taken at the problem.
As I see the situation at the moment, the minister has taken a new look at the pressure exerted upon him by the provinces, but it is not a very broad view. He has made modifications of the earlier agreements, but they are only modifications. I had hoped that a much larger view of the whole problem would have been taken and that the minister would have come forward with a more comprehensive suggestion. I realize that he has been patting himself on the back for the additional grants which are going to be made available to the provinces, the higher ceilings on the grants which will protect the provinces in case there is a turn for the worse in our economic conditions and the 8 per cent increase, as he puts it, in the revenues of the various provinces as a result of the increased amounts being available. The minister seems to be satisfied on that ground, but I must admit that he expressed some doubt that this plan will last without modification. I am sure it will have to be modified before too many years have gone by, because it is not possible to foresee all the problems which will arise.
I am always interested in the approach of cabinet ministers to the problems placed in front of them. A study of their speeches and expressions gives an inking of their philosophy. I should like to give three examples of this. In introducing the resolution yesterday the Minister of Finance seemed to be extremely hurried. It was difficult for us on this side to follow his remarks. I have just read them in order to get their full gist. The minister seemed to be a little anxious to get his resolution passed, or was not altogether satisfied with the proposition he was putting forward and hence was extremely hurried in his remarks. I should like to quote one sentence which he used, which appears on page 5987 of yesterday's Hansard:
The payments were on a more generous scale than before.
I notice the word "generous". That is the great white father making generous payments to those beneath him.

All right; the minister has now corrected that. Then as found at page 5988, the minister used this expression:
We have tried in every way to be sympathetic to the many legitimate provincial claims and at the same time reconcile them with our national responsibilities.

"Sympathetic"-another word that indicates that avuncular view of life. Why not simply say, "We have tried in every way to balance the legitimate claims of the provinces with the national responsibilities"? Let us not have this sympathetic attitude. Let us deal on a basis of equality. Similarly I notice that in the report of the proceedings of the federal-provincial conference of October 3, 1955, the Prime Minister used an expression which seems odd coming, as I think it did, from a prepared manuscript. It is to be found on page 15 of the proceedings, and the Prime Minister had this to say:
These advantages are of real value, but they are net benefits for which we must ask federal taxpayers to pay too high a price . . .
I did not realize that we had a particular class in our society who were federal taxpayers alone. I thought the taxpayer was just that chap who paid municipal taxes, provincial taxes and federal taxes all from the same pocket. If the thinking of the government is that there is a special class in the community called the federal taxpayer, I suggest that thinking should be revised.
The Minister of Finance doubted that the present proposal would last for all time, and with reason, because I am sure he has looked back at what has transpired in the past concerning the relationship between the dominion government and the provinces in connection with the division of their responsibilities and in connection with the amount of money available for each level of government to carry out its functions. Last year, speaking in the budget debate, I dealt with the subject of dominion-provincial conferences and traced the history of those conferences and the purpose for which they were devised. I noted that in the first 20 years following confederation there had been no interprovincial or dominion-provincial conferences, not that there was not dissatisfaction on the part of the provinces with regard to the financial arrangements made at the time of confederation but because no one took the initiative until about 1887.
For a period of 39 years from 1887 to 1926 there were a series of conferences called on the initiative of the provincial premiers to discuss matters of concern to them. There were seven of those conferences. I omit reference to the one called in 1918 by the then prime minister, Sir Robert Borden, in order to stimulate the war effort. The other conferences were called on the initiative of provincial premiers, and the subject matter of those conferences was very largely the question of financial assistance and a revision of the subsidies paid by the dominion government to the provinces under the terms of the confederation agreement.

So the problem is far from new in Canadian life, and the fact that it was not solved in those early years led us into the extreme difficulties of the depression years and resulted in the Rowell-Sirois report and finally in the tax rental agreements. But unless we are careful for the future we may again run into difficulty, and once again in Canadian history perhaps some of the areas of Canada will find themselves in an extraordinary depressed state and increased assistance will have to be given.
At some stage in Canadian history this matter must be grappled with, and though it cannot be settled in final terms improvements can be made. It is rather astonishing that 89 years after confederation there should be areas in Canada which are economically depressed in relation to other areas. The tempo of advance has not been the same all along the line, and apparently this has not been recognized from time to time. We have reached a period in national development when I think a much greater effort can be made to correct the disparities in our national life.
Ever since I have been here I have been hearing legitimate complaints from various areas of Canada with regard to the restraints that have been placed on their economic development, and I had hoped that now, having reached this stage, having to revise the tax rental agreements, a much greater effort would be made on the part of the government to correct these errors in our national life.
I spoke about the earlier conferences up to 1926. From that time to the present there have been another seven or so conferences called at the instance of the dominipn government, and called for a variety of purposes. A year ago last May when I was criticizing dominion-provincial conferences I objected to the nature of some of those conferences in the past and hoped that in the future the conferences would not take that turn. I pointed out that at one of the dominion-provincial conferences the delegates were advised that the purpose of the conference was to provide material for legislative programs for the legislatures as well as for the dominion. I recall that last year I objected to the Prime Minister announcing to the dominion-provincial conference the policy of the government with regard to unemployment, when it might better have been announced here in the House of Commons.
However, these later conferences, though dealing with a wide range of subjects, have nevertheless been compelled to deal with the same problem that affected the premiers in the earlier interprovincial conferences; how to solve the problem of meeting provincial

Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements responsibilities with the funds that were available to the provincial governments. That problem remains at the present time. In the conference that was assembled here last October the premiers in turn made their statements, and once again their recurring theme throughout the proceedings of that conference was that provincial responsibilities exceeded provincial sources of revenue, and the premiers asked that something be done about it.
Now we have the proposal of the Minister of Finance in order to come to grips with that problem. I think he is rather disappointed that his solution has not received wide acceptance, but it has not received wide acceptance because it has not gone far enough.
I think any solution evolved by dominion-provincial representatives will have to go much further than the one now before us. On its face it looks attractive. There is more money available for the provinces. There is greater protection offered to the less well off provinces. But the root of the matter has not been attacked, and that is the division of responsibility between the dominion government and the provincial jurisdictions. I note that last year I concluded my remarks in this way:
I will conclude with this statement. Dominion-provincial conferences may continue to be a necessity for Canada. If so, they should be restricted to the core of the problem, the division of administrative responsibility between the dominion and the provinces, and the division of fields of taxation.
That remains the core of the problem. The only way in which to approach that problem is by a conference which would deal with that crucial matter and deal with it not in 24 hours or in 48 hours but over a lengthy period. I believe we have reached the stage where we must reassess the effects of confederation and re-examine the responsibilities assigned to the various governments. We cannot continue on this basis of the dominion government putting forward, in the interests of the general advancement of Canada, various schemes which involve provincial participation on a financial basis, thereby increasing perhaps the load on provincial resources, without the assumption of full responsibility on the part of the dominion.
To my mind the best example of that, or perhaps not the best example but an easy example, is the question of the trans-Canada highway. On the surface it looks to be a fine scheme for the dominion government to say, "Canada is interested in communications. The trans-Canada highway, after the fashion on the great highways that criss-cross the United States, would be a good thing for

our country. This matter of highway construction is a provincial responsibility but the dominion government will assist. Let us now get together with the provinces and determine some plan of action." I do not know how many years it has been going on but it is a good many years, and we still have not completed the trans-Canada highway.
That is an example of the faltering steps this government has taken toward the solution of problems that happen to cross over into the provincial field. Why could it not be determined that the dominion government would accept full responsibility for something which has a national aspect of that character and which would be agreeable generally to the people of Canada? Why could the federal government not accept full responsibility for it and put that trans-Canada highway through? Have the provinces ever suggested that they would be opposed to having a first-class highway put through their territory without having to bear half the cost of construction of that highway? I think not.
I was interested in the October federal-provincial conference and in the remarks made by the premier of Manitoba, who is a good Liberal and who is, I think, sympathetic
__and I now use that word "sympathetic"
properly-to this dominion government because he has troubles somewhat similar to those of this government. I think he would like to help them out as best he could if they will help him out. Being in that frame of mind, he nevertheless was not too enthusiastic about some of the government's proposals, and he set forth very clearly the situation with regard to Manitoba. I thought some of these things might have been referred to by the Minister of Finance when he was introducing his resolution.
The premier of the province of Manitoba, as found at page 59 of this report, points out that the increase in government expenditure- and he is comparing the years 1945 and 1955 -was, for the federal government, 5-5 per cent whereas for the provincial governments the increase was 291-9 per cent and for municipal governments it was 276 per cent. Then the premier of Manitoba dealt with the question of capital investment and he showed the extent of the investment by the provinces and the municipalities. I quote his words as found at page 62:
Over the past five years, the provinces and municipalities between them have been spending nearly a billion dollars per year on capital projects of all kinds. The federal government has been spending perhaps half this amount annually. It is noteworthy that, in these post-war years of prosperity, the indebtedness of the provinces, municipalities and their agencies has risen from

$2-977 billion in 1945 to $5-715 billion in 1953-an increase of 92 per cent, while the federal government debt has actually been reduced from $18-438 billion to $18-276 billion.
So you have there a provincial premier pointing out the tremendous increase in the indebtedness incurred by those other governments, provincial and municipal, and the more satisfactory situation of the federal government. Then, dealing with that very matter, as found at page 63, he went on to say this:
This gives rise to the grave question of how the provinces and municipalities can hope to support much greater indebtedness in the next few years- an indebtedness which may well reach about $10 billion by 1961.
In other words the provinces see a great increase in their costs; and it is for that reason that they are not satisfied with the modest increase in their revenues which will result from the proposal of the Minister of Finance.
Earlier I mentioned the cross purposes which we sometimes find in Canada because of the overlapping of the dominion and provincial fields of activity. The premier of Manitoba gave an instance of that situation in dealing with what are called shared cost programs. He points out that although the provinces are appreciative of the initiative of the dominion government in putting forward these ideas concerning shared cost programs, nevertheless they create quite a burden for the provinces. He lists 15, I think, of these shared cost programs covering the fields of health and welfare, education and labour, public works, agriculture and natural resources. I quote his words as found at page 65:
In our fiscal year 1954-55 these programs involved expenditures amounting to more than $8,500,000. For the year in question this figure represented an amount equal to 15 per cent of Manitoba's budget.
In the list of these shared cost programs he queries the dominion's attitude toward an item such as civil defence, which apparently he would be happy to see taken over entirely by the dominion authorities.
He goes on, of course, to deal with the problem of education and the increasing burden on provincial and municipal resources as a result of the increased enrolment that is foreseen in all the schools and universities. Then he suggests, not an increase in the financial contribution from the dominion government of $115 million but that something in the nature of $200 million or $300 million a year would be a satisfactory increase. For example, he says this:
We think then, that the constructive approach to federal-provincial fiscal problems is to substantially expand the federal tax rental payments in the order of $200 million to $300 million a year. Further, if we are to rid ourselves of some of the

Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements.
clutter, uncertainty and inevitable interference' of the many shared cost programs, then the tax: rental payments should be increased by an additional $100 million to $150 million annually.
Now, Mr. Chairman, this sets out the problem rather briefly. The provincial governments and the municipalities are carrying: a greater share of the load in Canada than they are able to bear. Obviously if you study the statements by these various provincial premiers you will see that they feel there must be greater revenues available to the provinces. The method by which these revenues are made available, I concede, is something that can only be hammered out during long drawn out investigations and', studies. We have one method put before- us-now by the minister, and although that method in itself seems acceptable, the amounts involved are under criticism and properly so, because the real problem has not been approached; that is the division of responsibility in accordance with the change in our life in Canada. It is the responsibilities of governments in this country that require careful study.
Yesterday the Minister of Finance was telling us that over the last 20 or 25 years some progress has been made. One method has been tried out, tax rentals, and here is another method. I do not know whether he was implying that this should go along for another 20 years and then we should take another look at it. That is rather slow progress in 20 or 25 years, just one method being tried out. Now we have found that faulty and surely the present approach should be toward an investigation of the division of responsibility as between the dominion and provincial authorities. Can we suggest that a solution has been arrived at by way of this resolution and the bill that is going to follow it? It is a stop gap. to a certain extent, and it is a bit of a dole to-those provinces who have no bargaining power. Really, some of the poorer provinces have no bargaining power as against this strong dominion government. Fortunately there are in Canada some provinces which have bargaining power, and they have assisted their junior brethren by standing up to the dominion government and insisting on a better deal.
I do not like the idea of the dominion government taking the stand that they are handing out charity to the poorer provinces or taking this sympathetic approach to their problems or things of that nature. I think it is a question of sharing equally in this great country of ours, giving each part of it a fair share of the national wealth that is being produced, not by the dominion government and its policies so much as by the

Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements actions of the provincial and municipal authorities. The real work of the country is being done down at that level. The profits accruing from that work are being taken into the coffers at Ottawa. Then the authorities here seem to think that having received the profits from those activities, they were the producers of those profits.
That is not the view that is taken by the provincial and municipal authorities who have to provide the means by which the general industrial growth of this country takes place. They have to provide all the services that are ancillary to the development of industrial centres. They build access roads to develop our mines in the northern part of this country. They provide educational facilities and things of that nature. The profits come down to the central government, and then the central government thinks it has created all this wealth.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that a dominion-provincial conference be called devoted to the task of solving the division of responsibilities as between the dominion and provincial governments. It would have to continue for a considerable length of time because it is a difficult problem, but that is the only way we can reach a solution of this problem which has beset Canada ever since confederation.

Mr. Chairman, having in mind the considerations which I put before the committee last evening, as recorded on pages 6025 to 6028 of Hansard, considerations, including such matters as the moves already made in Canada, apparently directly aimed at weakening and ultimately destroying the British North America Act; having all these things in mind, one can be pardoned if he is tempted to wonder what the Minister of Finance is up to, he and the interests directing him from behind the scenes, granting there are such. Naturally we people in the opposition have to be aware of possibilities every time a move is made.
To the casual onlooker the resolution before the committee is innocent looking, innocuous in appearance, but this resolution could be, and probably is, designed to be a blank cheque in favour of Marxism. One of the great characteristics of Marxist philosophy is that very exacting taxation might be


applied. This will help to explain why I used the expression I have just used.
Most hon. members do not need to be reminded that there are evil forces abroad in the world. To those I referred last evening. That the agents of evil have manoeuvred themselves into high places is well known. From such agents of evil Canada is probably by no means free. Evidence of designing mischief-makers has been apparent in times past in Canada, more times than a few. Ours are days demanding the utmost vigilance because so many are talking centralization, as I pointed out last evening.
Let us look back over the past 30 years of our history. Thirty years ago it seems the efforts of the evil powers in Canada began to intensify. Consider briefly the passage of the Bank of Canada Act and events leading thereto. According to the testimony so ably and emphatically set forth by Sir Thomas White and Mr. Beaudry Leman in their memoranda of dissent, as they appear in the report of the Royal Commission on banking and currency for Canada, published in 1933, at pages 83 to 84 and 85 to 91 for Sir Thomas White, and at pages 95 to 97 for Beaudry Leman-according to these great Canadian authorities, Canada had about as much use for the Bank of Canada as a beaver would have for an extra tail. Why, then, was the Bank of Canada apparently forced upon Canada, and by whom and for whom and by what means?
More than a little light is thrown upon the situation by a more or less casual reference in a paragraph occurring in a letter dated January 14, 1941, by Hon. W. R. Motherwell, outstanding Saskatchewan statesman and at one time a member of this house. The letter was published in the Western Producer of January 23, 1941. In the letter Hon. W. R. Motherwell criticized the Sirois report. The passage in the paragraph to which I particularly refer reads as follows:
As the date of the dominion and provincial conference on the report of the Sirois commission draws nearer, the signs of systematic and increasing propaganda on behalf of the acceptance of this report becomes more and more bold, insidious and emphatic, e.g. that, as per press report, unless the seven or eight provinces that are said by the secretary of this commission to be bordering on defaulting on their bonds, accept this Sirois report, something "villainously destructive of our war efforts" is going to happen.
When the press of January 7 carried this remarkable statement by R. W. Fowler one of the secretaries of assistant secretaries of the Rowell-Sirois commission on dominion-provincial relations, it became quite apparent to even a blind man, that some one must have instructed him to make this, to me, quite unwarranted prediction and for the seeming purpose of coercing the Canadian provinces into the acceptance of this report by the application of stimulating doses of familiar propaganda dropped at appropriate times, places

and occasions to check a growing suspicion that to use an old adage "all was not gold that glitters'' throughout this much-lauded report. Mr. R. W. Fowler should remember that it is surely in vain for the fowler to spread the net in the sight of any bird (the Canadian provinces).
I understand from press dispatches that Premier Hepburn surmises that it was Ottawa (presumably the federal steering committee) that gave Mr. Fowler the tip what to say, but he denies it. Of course no one would expect the propagandist-inchief would admit this, even if it were entirely correct as a "safe" man would never admit anything like that or his name would be Dennis the next time a "safe" man's services were in demand.
Evidently a further study of this voluminous, potentially well seasoned with dynamite report, was desirable before accepting it blindly in wartime at the instance of one commission assistant secretary, while another had been busy filling up our magazines and press with even more alluring and seductive descriptive dope, than that which preceded the launching of that other anticipated farmer cure-all-the Bank of Canada.
. Hon. members who have heard that passage read I am sure will be impressed by such relics as those which are hidden away and which are to be found only in collections like the one which I happen to have been successful in accumulating a number of years ago.
But see now what is indicated by what this man says concerning the way in which the Bank of Canada was foisted upon the Dominion of Canada. There was an attempt to deliberately build up a public opinion in favour of the Bank of Canada. Now, if the Bank of Canada had been in demand by the people of Canada there would have been no need for the propaganda especially alluring, seductive and deluding such as occurred.
The reason I look upon this letter as being of more than usual significance is the fact that Hon. W. R. Motherwell was one of the finest public men, one of the finest statesmen who ever occupied a public position in the Dominion of Canada, either in a province or in the dominion, and he occupied both. He lived right through this period of which we are talking; he lived right through world war I; he lived right through the whole period during which the Bank of Canada was set up, and was living right through the time when the Rowell-Sirois report was being prepared to put before the people. He wrote this letter in the open forum of the Western Producer to draw to the attention of the people who might read it in western Canada the seriousness of the situation which was confronting the people at that time.
That passage from the pen of one of the really great Canadians merits most careful study and consideration. Notice the words "filling up our magazines and press with", and so forth, down to "Bank of Canada". You know, you do not get free access to our magazines and to our press so you can fill them up

And when a lot of money is behind anyone it is likely that he is not working for the welfare of the people; that has been proved over and over again. The Bank of Canada was represented-and I quote again the passage I read-as an;
. . . anticipated farmer cure-all.
The men who were advocating the Bank of Canada then knew perfectly well that the Bank of Canada would not cure the troubles of the farmers any more than it has done since. Our farmers are simply being crucified today, and what is the Bank of Canada doing? It is sitting with its hands serenely folded, incapable of doing anything about it and apparently not desiring to try to do anything about it.
Just imagine propaganda going out through the press in article after article after article assuring the farmers that once they got the Bank of Canada their troubles would all be ended. Just imagine what that means, Mr. Chairman. And then, after the propaganda had been going on long enough, when those who were engaged in sending out the propaganda thought they must have convinced the people, do you know what they began to do? They began to lie to the people in the maritimes, telling them that all the people out west were demanding this measure. Then they began to lie to the people in the west, telling them that all the people in the maritimes were demanding it, when the people had nothing to do with it at all. That is the sort of thing that went on in connection with the Rowell-Sirois report. Anyone who remembers those days will recall the coloured headlines an inch high which appeared in various newspapers all across the country.
The Bank of Canada was presented as a desirable institution, presented with-
. . . alluring and seductive descriptive dope.
-to use Mr. W. R. Motherwell's expression- in magazines and the press.
Somebody other than the common Canadian very much wanted the Bank of Canada, somebody with more than a little money and with quite above average influence with the press! There must be a good many hon. members in this house who know quite well who it is that exercises the greatest control over the daily press in our country. I have made references to that sort of thing in times past.
Now, the same or a similar somebody wanted the Rowell-Sirois report accepted. I think hon. members will find interesting an editorial which appeared in the Western Producer in the January 23, 1941, issue. I shall quote a number of small passages from

Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements that editorial; they are revealing to all who wish to get something resembling a comprehension of the kind of thing that was going on there. Here are some statements from the editorial. It is headed "The Interprovincial Conference". Remember that the Rowell-Sirois conference between the premiers and the prime minister of Canada had by that time been held. The article says:
The collapse of the dominion-provincial conference was the signal for the release in the press of western Canada of a flood of special dispatches and editorial comment, hysterical in tone and viciously mischievous in content. This would have been discreditable in peacetime; in wartime it is disgraceful and highly alarming. The dictionary is scoured for adjectives to damn the three premiers who refused to proceed with the conference on the terms laid down. They are treated as if they were rebels against constituted authority and the least of the accusations levelled at them is that they are archfomentors of disunity.
May I break in here to comment that these three men, Premier Hepburn of Ontario, Premier Pattullo of British Columbia and Premier Aberhart of Alberta were the three greatest figures of their time working for unity. I proceed with the editorial:
Be that as it may, it is our considered opinion that rarely in the history of Canada have the fires of disunity been more feverishly and effectively stoked than by the press of western Canada during the last few days. Throwing away all sense of restraint, without the shadow of an effort dispassionately to assess the merits of the disagreement, with an irresponsibility unmatched in the annals of journalism, the newspapers of western Canada-we have not yet seen those of the east-set themselves deliberately to fan the flames of discord by pouring contumely on provincial governments who dared disagree with them, and voicing open and convert threats of what is to happen to all the provinces from now on. All in all, in these days of travail, a sorry spectacle.
Having heard that passage I think the minister will forgive me if I have implied that he might be under the influence of people who are not working for the benefit of Canada. Here is another passage:
To those who followed the course of the Sirois commission since its appointment there should have been little cause for surprise in the final denouement. Mr. King's first announcement of his purpose was greeted with almost overwhelming criticism. Mr. Bennett-	'
Mr. Bennett was the leader of the Conservative party in the years following 1930, and I think he was one of the greatest figures who ever occupied a position in Canadian public life, notwithstanding what a good many people like to say about him. The article continues:
Mr. Bennett marshalled all the powers of his invective in his attack upon it-on the terms of reference, the method adopted and particularly the personnel selected. It was charged at the time that the common qualifications of the members of the commission were that they were all

Anybody who knows anything about the Canadian institute of international affairs knows that any person intimately connected with that organization is open to very definite suspicion indeed.

Those who remember the reception the commission received at some of the provincial capitals, particularly at Toronto and Edmonton, surely could not have been taken by surprise at what happened last week. Then as to the conference Itself. The press focuses attention on three provinces. Who might those hidden people be? I find a clue to that in the setting up of the Bank of Canada, to be found in the report of the royal commission on banking and currency in Canada which sat in 1933, which report I commend to the reading of hon. members of this house. That report is a perfect storehouse of information which bears most importantly upon us in these days.
Consider for a moment the members of that royal commission on banking and currency in Canada, 1933. I shall give their names so that hon. members can judge whether they would be men who would do a job for Canada. The first was Right Hon. Lord Macmillan, P.C., K.C., of the city of London, England. The city of London, England; what does that stand for? It stands for the concentration of financiers in England. In a very large measure those financiers are men of a blood which is alien to that of Anglo Saxon Celts, and they certainly are men who in no way are interested in the welfare of Anglo Saxon Celts. That has been proved over and over again, and it is still true.

I ask you who in his right senses in Canada would select two men from the city of London, England to come and sit in on a matter pertaining to the vital interests of Canada unless he were under pressure which he was unable to resist at the time.

speechtext: I will tell you in a minute what I am kicking about. What was the purpose of establishing the Bank of Canada? The main purpose of establishing the Bank of Canada, I submit, was to strangle and abolish the Finance Act of 1923, as well as to destroy the whole Canadian financial system as that system had been set up and developed by the fathers of confederation and succeeding Canadians under the British North America Act. In other words, the aim of setting up the Bank of Canada was to hew out a vast proportion of the foundation of the British North America Act by sweeping away at one fell swoop a financial system which had functioned with such admirable and enviable success up to and through world war I-I referred to this last night-and on down through the reconstruction period until the United States dragged Canada into the great depression of 1929 and the 1930's. Before I finish my speaking on this measure I am going to read from the evidence to show how splendidly Canada had done up to the time the Bank of Canada was established.
Why establish the Bank of Canada if thought was given to Canada's welfare? The commission was set up on July 31, 1933, as is indicated at page 5 of the report, and its devastating and sweeping recommendation was submitted on September 27, 1933, as indicated at page 82 of the report. In other words this body of men determined in so short a period, as I have indicated by these dates, upon a recommendation that went far toward undermining the British North America Act. The Balfour declaration of 1926, which said that members of the British commonwealth now were equal in every aspect of their internal and external affairs, was undermined by the setting up of the Bank of Canada; and the statute of Westminster of 1931 was also undermined all by reason of the fact that the Bank of Canada brought Canada's financial system in indefinite measure under foreign, if not alien control.
There are those who say that this is not the case. All you have to do is read the evidence recently given by the governor of the Bank of Canada at the hearing we had before the standing committee on banking and commerce. You will see how very cagey and cautious he was, and how he replied once or twice to the effect that if the government asked certain things the bank simply would not agree. Look at what happened to our price structure.
