Mr. Chairman, in speaking on the resolution today I want to take one phase of dominion-provincial relations, education. This is supposed to be a very delicate subject because we are told, especially by the government, that any grants to the provinces in aid of education would be an invasion of provincial rights. I believe we have reached a very real and very serious crisis in education. To say that federal aid would be an invasion is like a fire chief telling an Englishman that he cannot go into his house to put out a fire because an Englishman's home is his castle.
It is true that under the British North America Act the provinces have exclusive jurisdiction over education. That is the way it is and that is the way we want it, but it seems to me that does not stop the federal government from giving a helping hand this year anyway, from the large estimated surplus of money that has already been paid by the taxpayers. Health is another item under provincial jurisdiction as set out in the British North America Act, but you do not hear the Minister of National Health and Welfare being particularly quiet about the grants he is giving to the provinces to help them to build hospitals, and there does not seem to be any undue modesty or embarrassment about the suggested health scheme which would be contributed to both by the provinces and the federal government. Certainly there have been no complaints from the provincial governments with regard to the grants that have been given for hospitals.
Therefore I do not believe it would be an invasion in any way, because education has gone far beyond the lower levels of government. When the British North America Act was drawn up children were educated and trained for life in their own local communities, but today children must be educated and trained for life in the whole country, in fact for life in the whole world. In a book published earlier this year entitled "Canadian Education Today" there is this observation:
Education is a function of the province, a responsibility of the community and the concern of the whole nation.
I believe that education is an essential social service today. It is just as essential to the federal government as it is to the local or provincial governments. After a survey by the Canadian school trustees association last year, this statement was made:
Much of the cost of the local school is due to national requirements. National defence demands that the basic education in all parts of the

dominion be thorough and extensive. Canada's development as an industrial nation can continue as it should only if local schools provide the basic education for scientifically trained personnel. Technical education must be provided for an increasing percentage of youth.
Education has taken on a national significance since the fathers of confederation drew up the British North America Act. The type of schooling that was adequate 50 years ago is no longer good enough. I believe that our education is falling below acceptable standards. The criterion, unfortunately, is dollars and cents, and it certainly is a wrong criterion. If our educational standards are falling below acceptable levels, then not the least of the sufferers will be the federal government. As the trustees association said, the federal government is dependent upon the provinces and the municipalities for the basic general education of the people it needs, including engineers, civil servants, armed forces personnel, scientists-yes, and cabinet ministers too. Education is of such national importance that the federal government should make certain that it is not allowed to fall below acceptable standards. I think we all feel that education is becoming a grave national problem, and no small part of local school costs is due to national requirements. Indeed, schooling has taken on a national significance.
Earlier this year the President of the United States called in representatives of some 300 organizations to participate in a conference on education. I think that would be a good idea for us to follow. The vice president of the United States recognized at that conference the national importance of education when he asserted that it was education that determines the quality of our statesmen who are endeavouring to keep peace. It is education that determines the character and leadership of our religious men who are responsible for our spiritual standards. It is education that determines the character and leadership of management and labour, of our cultural life and of those who will determine this nation's future, the electors themselves.
Vice President Nixon said at that time: We should recognize that some additional federal activity and responsibility is inevitable and necessary in the field of education.
I believe that Canadians must recognize this realistic fact too, and I do not believe that education grants from the federal government would in any way threaten provincial rights in education. Canada is richly endowed with great natural and human resources. It has been pointed out by many of our intellectual leaders that we are concerned more with our natural resources than we are with our human resources. Education is the main tool necessary for developing a country's
17, 1956	6071
Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements human resources, and I believe the time has come when the federal government must help fashion that tool and then the provincial governments will finish the job.
My interest in the problem of education is not purely academic. In the House of Commons I represent a suburban constituency where education is becoming an ever-increasing burden. We have a shortage of classrooms and a shortage of teachers. Communities are springing up overnight and schools are too small even before their construction is finished. Classrooms are so crowded that the hours have to be staggered so that all children in the communities can go to school. This is true of my constituency, and I am sure it is true of many parts of Canada. The school population is increasing at the rate of 150,000 a year. In 1951 there were 2| million school children in Canada. Today there are 3| million students enrolled in the elementary and secondary schools. Five years from now this situation will be even more complex and certainly the schools will be more crowded. As of June 1, 1956, there were 97 per cent more children under the age of five years than there were on June 1, 1941. Every one of those children must be given a good education; every one of them must be given a good education free. We believe that is the right of every Canadian child.
Even today education is one of our biggest problems, and it will become greater in the future. I believe it must be faced by all levels of government. Up to date the federal government just shrugs it off with a holier than thou attitude on the basis that it would be interfering with provincial rights if it were to do anything. Local governments are the poor relations with respect to the tax dollar, yet local governments carry most of the education burden. Municipalities are paying 65 per cent of education costs and the provinces are paying 35 per cent.
This really means that the home owner is carrying almost the complete tax load with respect to education, yet education goes far beyond the local community. Young people, wherever they are from Newfoundland to British Columbia, are being educated not for one municipality or for one province but for the whole of Canada. But it is the home owner who is paying two-thirds of the school costs.
Then, too, this system of financing education at the local level certainly fosters inequalities in education. Some communities have more tax resources than others, and some communities can have better teachers and better schools. At the present time there are 5,142 untrained teachers teaching in our

Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements schools and 3,744 partially trained teachers. It seems to me that this is a very bad situation, and one which is going to get worse. We boast of equal educational opportunity for all Canadian children; but again, because of dollars and cents, the opportunity is not equal.
A few years ago there came out a little book by George Orwell called "Animal Farm" and in it he made this sardonic observation:
All pigs are equal but some are more equal than others.
So it is with respect to our educational opportunities; some are more equal than others across Canada. The trustees association has stressed this fact by pointing out that all children do not have equal opportunities to get an education and that they are dependent on the taxpaying ability of the district in which they live. It is true that money cannot buy education. However, it can supply the tools; and the quality of education depends upon the teaching or upon the quality of those tools. The highest quality of teaching should be and could be available to all Canadian children. If the federal government would assume its share of educational costs, there would be equal opportunities for all children to get an education.
I have dealt only with the elementary and secondary school education because they are of vital concern to the people in my constituency. But as everyone knows, higher education is shaping up as an even greater problem for us to face in the future. In the past young people could earn enough money during the summers to put themselves through university. Today such a thing is impossible. If they earn enough to pay their fees they are lucky.
In May of this year the University of Toronto was obliged to raise its fees by 11-2 per cent and Dr. Sidney Smith, the president of the university has indicated that it probably will not stop there. Higher education should be available to all who have ability, and not just to those who have the ability to pay for it. At the rate we are going, higher education may well become just a rich man's privilege in this country. In a brief presented to the royal commission Dr. Sidney Smith summed up the situation in these words:
University courses are still much too expensive for a great many of our population. Equality of opportunity is a fine-sounding phrase; it will not be a fact in our democracy until the universities can enrol able students irrespective of the financial situation of their parents.
Tuition fees have been raised repeatedly in recent years . . . We have not been receiving from governments financial support that is worthy to be compared with what universities receive in Great Britain or the United States.

Mr. Chairman, I believe the time has come when the federal government must find a means of paying its share of the cost of this essential service, namely education.

Mr. Chairman, one of the particular reasons we oppose this present resolution was expressed by the leader of our party the other day, when he stated that this bill is being passed without receiving the approval of the provinces. The government is now proposing to write into legislation something which the provinces may not accept. By doing so they are contributing to what we regard as an undesirable principle, namely the principle of the centralization of government or the centralization of power. That is a principle that is contrary to what we deem to be our free democratic way of life.
I think I can say that this central government now seated at Ottawa has become extremely powerful over the last few years with all the legislation it has been able to build up around it. Almost all the legislation which it proposes has the effect of solidifying its policies not only in the industrial world but in the economic and monetary fields. The more power that is given to governments, the less power remains in the hands of the people. We believe that a government should give a lead but that it should never impose its will. This resolution which precedes a bill has all the earmarks of attempting to impose the will of this government upon the provinces.
Once again I say that for democracy to function properly a government should lead, not impose its will. We in the Social Credit movement believe in the autonomy of the provinces. We do not believe we can go wrong in attempting, at every hand, to protect the rights of the provinces. One reason we believe that is that the provinces are nearer the individual than the centralized government at Ottawa. Once again I say I do not believe we can go wrong in principle by protecting the autonomous rights of the provinces.
I do not think we need to go very far abroad to recognize that this principle of the autonomy of the provinces is acceptable to the people of the provinces and the people of Canada as a whole. I think Mr. Duplessis is an example of that, for he has had remarkable success in winning elections on the basis of his determination to protect the autonomy and rights of his own province. Whether or not we agree with his platform in provincial elections is another matter. I am only saying this to illustrate that the people themselves are supporters of provincial autonomy. They do not like the central

government, living a long way from them, dictating what their particular provincial government should do.
I believe that is where we differ with our C.C.F. friends. I listened very carefully to the speech given the other day by the leader of the C.C.F. party. In my opinion it savoured of centralization. He indicated that this government must have the power to do certain things. Our position is that this government should be in a position to lead the provinces in such a way that the provinces can do certain things for themselves.
This government has boasted of the high economic level that presently exists in Canada. They boast of their surpluses. They say that Canada has never had it as good as it is today. They appear to me, at least, to take all credit to themselves for what we will admit is a fairly high economic level.
Let me remind you, Mr. Chairman, that the provinces have been largely responsible for this high level of economic activity in this country. It is the provinces who have encouraged investment in business enterprises within their boundaries. I say, therefore, that the provinces have been largely responsible for the high level of business activity in this country. Ontario and Quebec are the two mainly industrial provinces of Canada. They have so managed their affairs that perhaps they have attracted industries over the years. Nevertheless those two great industrial provinces are managing their own industrial expansion. This central government has very little to do with the encouragement of business enterprise in the various provinces, unless of course it is in the awarding of certain defence contracts to certain Arms who may operate within those two particular provinces.
Let us take Alberta as another very prosperous province. What has this government done to actually encourage the development of that province? Surely some credit is due to the present local administration in Alberta for the high economic level we find in that province. Well, so far as I am able to observe many of our Liberal friends have gone out in an attempt to destroy the policies of that government, which in the last couple of decades has virtually built that province into a new economic power. Therefore surely the provinces have some credit coming to them for the high economic level which Canada is enjoying today. My leader says, "the major part of it". I should not depreciate my remarks by saying the Alberta government have some reason to take some credit. I think they deserve practically all the credit,
Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements for they are the ones who encouraged investment in business expansion and in the exploitation of their natural resources in order that the province may benefit thereby.
Let us take British Columbia, for instance, and the great expansion that has taken place there over the past few years, and I am bold enough to say since the election of the present Social Credit government of that province. I picked up the Financial Post of March 17 and found one section in that paper devoted to the great expansion that is going on in the province of British Columbia.
Let me ask what part this central government at Ottawa has been playing in that respect. Here I find a full page of articles headed, "Prancing prosperity of Canada's west coast". I like that caption. It is prancing like a healthy steed, ready to win a race; and it is going to win, believe me. That is the first page. Here is the second page, "How and where B.C. industry is going". Mr. Hansel!: I say once again, Mr. Chairman, and I am using these illustrations as illustrations to prove the point, the high economic level that is being experienced in Canada today is almost entirely due to the provinces themselves encouraging the expansion of industry.
Now, Mr. Chairman, there is one policy over which this government has almost complete control, and that is the monetary policy of the country. Those provinces have been able to expand not because of the monetary policy that this government is pursuing but in spite of the financial policy this government is pursuing. If this government were pursuing the right and proper financial policy, those provincial governments could expand industry in the provinces without a terrific trail of debt and excessive taxation.
The municipalities in those provinces find it very difficult to get through without excessive taxation which is almost breaking the backs of the taxpayer. The other day I had a letter from a group in the town of Nanton, an average-size community in my own constituency. They had set up a committee to investigate the possibility of bringing industry to that little town. Why? Because they felt that in order to relieve the tax burden of the people the town would be better off if it could have some industries established there. Let me ask what this government has done to encourage the establishment of small industries in any small communities? Why, they hardly know that those small communities exist until it is income tax collection time, and then they know because they send their inspectors around to see that the individual taxpayer is not beating the government out of a few dollars of taxes. In saying this, I am not countenancing for one moment the idea that anyone should evade the just laws of the country. When municipalities find difficulties in getting through without imposing almost unbearable taxation upon the people it is because the individual taxpayer himself has difficulty in getting through. And here is where we come to the monetary policy which this government is pursuing. Not only does it leave the provinces in a difficult financial position to get through, but it leaves the municipalities in a difficult position to get through, and it leaves the individual taxpayer in a very difficult position in order to make both ends meet in his common, ordinary everyday spending for the necessities of life.
If this government were pursuing a proper economic policy, the people would not have to go so heavily in debt and mortgage the future in order to live. Let me put it to you in this way, Mr. Chairman. These

provinces have encouraged industry to-develop within their own boundaries. Industries have developed; industries have produced the goods. They go on sale and people buy those goods. Coming from the process of industry is a certain amount of money that is distributed to the people in the form of wages, in the form of profits,, in the form of dividends, and so forth. Since the provinces have encouraged industry, and by reason of that encouragement, the national income has reached a certain level.
This government then comes along and capitalizes on the effective operation of provincial governments in encouraging industry, and this government then receive their revenues from that prosperity which has been mainly due to some of the provinces-encouraging industry. Very well; not only is this government enabled thereby to build up surpluses in their treasury, but let it be remembered that the individual taxpayer who buys the products of industry finds that he has not enough money to be able to buy those products of industry. The result is that if they want to acquire the products of industry they have to go into debt to acquire them. We find that instalment buying in Canada today has reached almost $2J billion. I have the exact figure here somewhere. It does not make any difference; it is well over $2 billion. Just what does this mean? It means that where the taxpayer has gone into instalment buying to the tune of over $2 billion he has mortgaged his future income to that amount. It means that his future income is not then able to buy the products of industry that are now coming off the assembly lines because his income has been hypothecated to pay for something that came off the assembly lines a year or two years ago. Of course, it leaves the taxpayer that much short in his present income to buy the products of industry today. Why is he left short? He is left short by reason of the fact that the monetary policy of this government is of such a nature that it never provides the consumer public of this country with the purchasing power to buy back the products of industry. So here we have the taxpayer short in his income, owing bills for things that he has bought on the instalment plan, and he also finds himself with his nose to the grindstone in order to get enough money to pay the various taxes that are imposed upon him. It is most improper to tax everything the wage earner has to buy. Regardless of what he wants to do he has to pay a tax on it. If he wants to get married he has to buy a licence; that is a tax. If he wants to own a dog he has to pay a dog tax.

Not to the federal
government.

If an individual wants to buy anything he has to pay a sales tax. Regardless of what he wants to do or buy there is a tax somewhere which he must pay and what he has left to live on is very little. Surely in a country the size of this with its vast wealth of natural resources and industrial production the people should have incomes sufficient to permit them to pay their way.
I picked up a paper the other day and I have brought it with me with a view to referring to it by way of comparison. The material on the front page struck me rather forcibly. On the front page of the Ottawa Citizen of Saturday, July 14, 1956 is a large aerial view photograph of a highway which is being built in Germany. The picture is captioned "This is not Carling Avenue" and beneath the caption the following appears.
An eye-catching pattern is formed by the new Autobahn highway junction, Germany's biggest and most modem, outside Frankfurt. The clover-leaf in the background connects the Berlin-Munich, Cologne-Nuernberg and Munich-Kassel-Hamburg highways. The junction in the foreground serves traffic to and from Frankfurt. The circle in the lower right is in front of the Frankfurt airport entrance. Built in a year, the giant junction was opened to traffic on July 10, closing the link in Germany's vast Autobahn system.
I mentioned that picture today simply to indicate what has been done in a country that was supposed to have been dead broke. Germany went through a war and was overwhelmingly defeated, its industries were destroyed and its cities demolished. I was in Germany not too many years ago and I took a trip to some of the devastated cities which had been levelled to the ground. Within the space of a few years Germany has been able to build up its industrial cities to a point where it has now become a strong competitor in the markets of the world.
I realize that I cannot deal with the work of the federal district commission here but I would like to mention that I have been sitting as a member of that committee and we have been told that their plans will be finalized 25 years from now. Surely there is something wrong with the management of the affairs of this nation as compared to some other nations when a country as well equipped as ours requires 25 years to complete a project and yet a nation that was supposed to have been dead broke following an ignominious defeat in war was able to complete a project such as this within a few months. It is time that the government accepted a little advice from some other people and some other parties in this country, and I am bold enough to say it

Only the Social Credit party.
Well, we come closest to it.

As we sit here in this house what do we find? The government brings down legislation; they know it all and that is it. The opposition tries to point out the weaknesses in it and proposes certain remedies; but, oh no, if it is proposed by any member of any opposition party it is never acceptable to the government. Let us know what province has written to the government and said, "Here, we favour that resolution; go ahead."
That would never happen.

I am very glad, Mr. Chairman, that you informed me my time has expired because as I look at the notes I hold in my hand I see the word "conclusion" and I am forced to sit down. I repeat, Mr. Chairman, that we are opposed to the principle of centralization as depicted in this resolution.

Mr. Chairman, first of all let me assure you that I have no newspapers to read to tell you about the wonderful expansion that is taking place in the province of Ontario and I have no notes here indicating when I should conclude my remarks, and therefore it may well be that I shall ramble a little bit today. Perhaps one of the reasons I might ramble will be explained by my initial comment in that I feel there is very little new which I can offer in this debate. I have no apologies to make for that because it seems to me that the only way to get across to the government the plight of the provinces, and more particularly the plight of the municipalities, is to repeat over and over the situation which confronts those levels of government. As a matter of fact I am surprised that more attention has not been paid to some of the problems which affect our municipalities. As I said once before, I have noted in the Parliamentary Guide the wide municipal and board of education experience which a great number of hon. members possess. However, once they arrive here the great federal problems that confront them apparently bury in their minds the real problems which they left in their municipalities.
It has been emphasized before, but I want to say again, that during a period of stress and strain of war we expect a trend, in these days at least, toward centralization, and I might use the term autocracy, in government. This method has been used in order to get things done. It is not a method, but rather an excuse to get things done. As a result many of the problems facing the municipalities and provinces are submerged in the over-all attitude that is adopted.


But when peace comes-I say this advisedly, notwithstanding the great problems which face the Minister of National Defence at the present time-there is a great necessity to return to a system of government which is more decentralized, which comes closer to the people, which gets down to the grass roots and enables the municipalities and the provinces to provide an expansion of services for industry which in effect will raise the standard of living and make the tax load easier as far as all levels of government are concerned.
I think that one of the major problems facing us right now in connection with this legislation is the difficulty of convincing the government that the stage of centralization and autocracy which found its place in a period of emergency is over, and it is about time we returned to the people who are closest to the tax dollar sufficient tax revenue to enable them to expand their economy.
This is a serious problem and I am not going to deal with it at length because we are going to have an opportunity to look at the legislation during its subsequent phases. However, I was most impressed with the remarks of the hon. member for York-Humber who said she represented a suburban constituency which was part of metropolitan Toronto and that the great problem which was confronting that area was the one having to do with education. I think that that represents one of the major problems in so far as the obtaining of necessary tax funds is concerned. The hon. member mentioned in that connection that 65 per cent of the amount required came from real property with 35 per cent coming from the province. The major load falls upon the home owner and this creates a major problem.
Just the other day I received as a taxpayer a letter from the clerk's department of the township of Etobicoke, which is one of the three municipalities which make up the constituency of York West. This letter is written in a rather apologetic manner but it points out the problem that is created by educational costs and what the municipality is running up against. The letter reads:
This letter is written to bring the matter of multiple occupancy in single family areas to the attention of all home owners and explain as clearly as possible the scope of the zoning by-law in respect to occupancy and the necessity for the enforcement of said provisions.
I skip a few words.
1. Scope: The township building and health regulations provide further that no cellar shall be used as habitable space and this restriction applies to all cellars regardless of zone.
The contravention of these by-laws by a minority of the property owners affects not only

the adjacent properties but also the economy of the township as a whole in many ways including the following:
The letter goes on to set out the ways in which this affects the standards of the community, and then there is this paragraph:
(3) Additional families in a dwelling require additional services such as sewage disposal and garbage collection which obviously must be paid for. In this respect, however, the financial effect is most apparent when educational costs are considered which at present are approximately $225 per pupil in public school and $425 in secondary school.
The Minister of Finance may say that that is a particular problem affecting a small part of my constituency, that if there are people living in a zoned area which does not permit multiple occupancy that is no concern of his. But I would point out that from the municipal standpoint it is absolutely essential that every person be accounted for in connection with this requirement of $225 per pupil in our public schools and $425 per pupil in our high schools. Unless everyone is accounted for the money for educational purposes is not going to be available.
What will happen is that many of these people who might be quite happy to contribute their share of the educational costs are going to have to go out on the housing market. We will be confronted with a situation which is entirely different from the attitude taken in connection with financial responsibility. The government has been telling us that housing is going along fine, but the fact is that we are faced with a restriction in the granting of credit for the building of houses. Regardless of what is said by those who sit on the treasury benches, it is quite obvious to anyone who is close to the market that it is becoming more and more difficult to build necessary houses. In fact at the present time it is almost impossible to build houses that people can afford to buy.
Here is a situation where people are being put out of housing accommodation because of the necessity of eking out the last dollar which the municipality can make available for educational purposes. At the same time they are being told that there is no place for them to go. That indicates how serious the situation is at the present time. Unless more attention is paid to an equitable distribution of the tax load in connection with education we are going to be faced with a lowered standard of education. That is the last thing we want to have happen in this country.
What do we do about it? I do not know. We have had conference after conference in connection with the distribution of taxes and we do not seem to be accomplishing very much. I am wondering whether the
Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements people from the federal government who sit around that table realize that they are continuing the grasping attitude which they adopted during a wartime economy. It seems to me it is about time that they approached it in a new way or it will be too late to assist these people at the level of municipal taxation. The last time I spoke about this I mentioned that the situation was serious because we can get back to the position we were in during the depression when municipalities could not meet their obligations and there was default. As a matter of fact, I have read several headlines in local newspapers indicating that people were already being put in a position where they were forced to sell their homes and move farther and farther afield to escape this type of taxation.
Therefore I think my leader was quite right when he suggested that there should be a reconvening of this dominion-provincial group and that a new approach might be made to a more permanent type of solution. For my part I have said before that I do not think we will have a true attack on the economy of government until the time when the people who actually spend the money collect it. I do not mean by that that they must set up the mechanical means of doing it, but I think that somewhere along the line when collection is made it must be obvious that the money is being collected for certain purposes. Someone will say that the dominion government has always been in that position. Fortunately for them they are in the happy position of always being able out of their revenues to balance any detrimental effect on the public by saying we have got a new deal for you, we have got an increase of some kind in some type of allowance, we are going to introduce a new type of pension or we have got up our sleeve a new type of health insurance. In that way they are able to get a shot in the arm because the people say that they are collecting these taxes for purposes that are very good for the country. But along the line there will have to be a solid approach to the basis of collection of moneys and the spending by the same agency. Let us hope, as I said before in paraphrasing Mark Twain, that we will not all continue to talk about municipalities and do nothing about them.

Mr. Chairman, in taking part in the debate on the resolution now before us I should like to begin my remarks with a paragraph from a history book entitled "Building the Canadian Nation" by George W. Brown. The paragraph is as follows:
I see in the not remote distance one great nationality bound, like the shield of Achilles, by the blue rim of ocean. I see it quartered into

many communities, each dispensing of its internal affairs, but all bound together by free institutions, free intercourse and free commerce. I see within the round of that shield the peaks of the western mountains and the crests of the eastern waves, the winding Assiniboine, the fivefold lakes, the St. Lawrence, the Ottawa, the Saguenay, the Saint John and the basin of Minas. By all these flowing waters, in all the valleys they fertilize, in all the cities they visit in their courses, I see a generation of industrious, contented, moral men, free in name and in fact, ever capable of maintaining in peace and in war a constitution worthy of such a country.
Those were the words, Mr. Chairman, of D'Arcy McGee on the day when Canada was born. I am sure that those words expressed not only the hopes and the views of D'Arcy McGee but the hopes that were in the minds of all those great Canadian statesmen who, beckoned on by that glorious vision, cast aside their prejudices and worked together to achieve union of the provinces into the federal state as we now have it. We are privileged to view their labours from the vantage point of history. We can appreciate the prophetic vision which inspired them. We can share in the fulfilled dreams of a united Canada and we can also contribute something to the enhancing of those ties which bind together those of varying racial origins, religious beliefs and political persuasions.
As we turn back to history we find that some of the factors which were instrumental in the bringing together of the nation into confederation are outlined. I have read, for instance, of the civil war in the United States. Following the victory achieved by the northern forces some of the extremists expressed the view that their next objective should be the conquest of Canada and the freeing of the entire North American continent from British domination. Because of the expression of those views the early statesmen believed that in order to maintain an effective defence it was necessary that the provinces of Canada bind themselves together in union. One of these men, George Etienne Cartier, said:
If we desire to obtain England's support for our defence we must help ourselves. When we are united the enemy will know that if he attacks any province he will have to deal with the combined forces of the empire.
Defence was one of the factors that inspired these men to work towards the achievement of the union of the provinces. Trade was another factor. A crisis in government affairs more or less brought the whole situation to a head. Then we find in subsequent pages of history how the maritime provinces gathered together and had a conference to discuss the question of maritime union. At that conference some delegates were present from the Canadas, and as the discussions


progressed they had a vision. A vision was born of something greater than maritime union, and that was the union of all the provinces of Canada.
The result was that a further conference was held in Quebec when resolutions were drawn up with the aim of providing a strong national government while at the same time leaving the provinces free to control matters within their own borders. We are all acquainted no doubt with the history of what happened and how that conference led to the London conference attended by 16 delegates. They used the resolutions drawn up at the Quebec conference as their working papers. They presented their findings, and the result was that the British North America Act was passed by the British parliament. So we find that through a process of negotiation, conferences and finally agreements Canada as a federal state was brought into being.
I think we should have appreciation for the achievements of the past. Just a short time ago we saw portrayed on television the history of confederation, and I am sure that we shared some of the pride of belonging to such a country as ours. I believe that the preservation of confederation is a matter of primary concern at the present time. Because of that belief I would sound a warning, as other speakers have sounded warnings, that the procedures followed by the present administration are tending towards a breakdown of that very same confederation that we so much cherish. By legislation, by practice, by economic pressures-in all of these ways-I fear that we are coming to the place where confederation may be getting into a rather shaky position instead of being strengthened with the passage of the years.
We find that the provinces themselves are taking a very dim view of many of the activities of this present administration. I have here in my file a number of newspaper clippings. I am not going to take time to read them all, but I am just going to refer to them because I feel that they indicate some of the feeling of the provinces with regard to the attitude of the federal government toward the provinces and toward provincial autonomy.
I have here a clipping from the Ottawa Citizen of February 24, 1955. I know we do not like to be reminded of these things, and I know some would say the very fact that we express these thoughts and refer to them tends to aggravate the situation. However, I am not in agreement with that deduction. The title of this article is "Overtones of secession in Angry P.E.I. House" and it reads in part as follows:

An angry murmur of maritime discontent with overtones of secession sounded Thursday in the legislature of Canada's tiniest province.
Opposition leader R. R. Bell told the Prince Edward house the province is getting "a miserable deal from Ottawa". If it continues unity would be undermined. He said that since 1873, the year the province joined confederation, "we've had nothing but blood, sweat and tears."
Then further on in the article, referring to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration and one of his statements, Mr. Bell had this to say:
If he-
That is referring to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration.
-was to come over here and say we couldn't leave confederation, I'd tell him "who is going to stop us."
That, I must say, is by the Canadian Press.
The Ottawa Journal of June 21, 1955, contains large black headlines "Smallwood Would Secede", under which appears an article which reads in part as follows:
Premier Joseph Smallwood threatened last night to lead Newfoundland out of confederation with Canada unless the federal government stopped discriminating against the four Atlantic provinces, including his own .	.	. His threat of quitting
Canada was given added weight by the presence of Premier Henry Hicks of Nova Scotia, a Liberal, and Premier Hugh John Flemming of New Brunswick, a Conservative. Flemming introduced Smallwood in glowing terms and Hicks praised him for "talking the way we should in the Atlantic provinces".
Then I go to a brief paragraph further down in the article where I find the following in quotation marks indicating that they are Mr. Smallwood's own words:
"Before we become second-class citizens of Canada, we will show the other maritime provinces how to get out of confederation." There was a storm of applause from the audience.
Mr. Chairman, it does not look as though the foundation of confederation were being strengthened very much when provinces and provincial premiers would give expression to such views and would threaten, if the situation continued, to lead their provinces out of confederation.
I have before me a clipping from the Ottawa Journal of Saturday, April 14, 1956. It is headed "Maritime premiers critical of Ottawa". I am just going to read one or two very brief statements:
Premier Flemming said as far as New Brunswick is concerned the new agreement is worse for the province than the old one.
Another paragraph reads as follows:
Mr. Matheson said his province probably fares the worst of all under the new scheme. Premier Hicks said if his province's proposal to equalize taxation payments had been accepted all three maritime provinces would have benefited.

Again I say, Mr. Chairman, that when we have expressions like that, where we find that people are not only thinking in this way but are voicing the opinions that the province could probably secede, we have evidence that the proposals themselves which have been presented to the governments were far from satisfactory. I would suggest that right across Canada there is a growing feeling that the dominion government are not playing fair with the provinces. They are centralizing more and more power and authority here in the federal government; they are assuming more power; they are trying to wield greater influence. All this is far from bringing comfort to the provinces in their particular situations.
I think that this resolution and the draft agreement that we have tabled some time ago indicate a failure on the part of the federal government properly to assess the position of the provinces in these proposals. During the course of the debate reference has been made to a number of important factors indicating the ever increasing demands that are being made on the provincial and municipal authorities. Reference has been made to education. A number of members have spoken of this particular phase of our national life. The leader of the official opposition stated that the situation could possibly result_ in tragedy. So as we face that particular issue and as we see the ever-increasing demands being made upon the provincial and municipal authorities with regard to education, we can see that the proposals that are being presented to the provinces are far from adequate to meet the challenge of these increasing costs.
Reference has been made to road cons;ruction. I know that the Minister of Finance referred to the fact that $82 million had been paid out thus far as the federal government's share of the cost of construction of the trans-Canada highway. In view of the fact that every province is facing the tremendous program of expansion and in view of the importance of adequate roads and transportation facilities, I would suggest that the $82 million is a very small part for the federal government to pay toward these increasing costs. I would also suggest that because of the building of roads-access roads to the natural resources, and roads of every description-the country is being opened up with the result that great new sources of revenue are being opened to the federal government. Yet, in spite of that fact, the federal government refuses to assume the additional cost or to share the additional cost so that the provinces can continue to develop in the way they should develop. As to the development of national resources and the cost of health

Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements and welfare, I know that the federal government has assumed some share, but I suggest that that share is extremely small indeed in comparison with the needs that exist.
Another problem that we face to quite an extent is that of conservation. I know that in British Columbia, in my own riding to a great extent, we are faced with a problem of trying to save for agricultural purposes what little arable land we have. The rivers are gradually eating it away. Yet when we present the matter to the federal government, what do we find? I know we received some assistance in the past.
I was rather disconcerted the other day to receive a letter from one of the municipalities saying the federal government had refused to pay anything towards the cost of protection there this year. I have not had time to discuss it with the Minister of Public Works, but I certainly will. Let me just refer to one particular section to which I have referred earlier. I see the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources is in his seat and he will recall my reference to this matter on a number of occasions. It concerns the flood danger existing in the Vedder river area. I have made repeated requests and my predecessor made repeated requests; the provincial minister of agriculture has been down here presenting the matter and showing aerial photographs, but yet the federal government cannot see its way clear to assuming any responsibility. They say it is not within their jurisdiction but let me state that according to the information we have the section up above where this particular situation exists was, up until about 1930, part of the federal railway belt. The federal government up until 1930 received in excess of $400,000 by way of stumpage and royalties from timber removed from that area. This does not take into consideration what the government received through income tax and corporation taxes. They received revenues, Mr. Chairman, but when it came to the matter of assuming responsibility they said, "We have not any responsibility; that is something the provinces have to face." Certainly, it is resented.
In 1953 the province of British Columbia presented to the government of Canada a brief on federal-provincial co-operation in economic development. It is a very interesting brief and covers many of the great problems and projects that faced the provincial government in those days just after they had taken office. The premier, minister of finance and the attorney general came to Ottawa and presented the brief. What was the result, what were the effects? Well, we have not seen them. I suppose the cabinet listened to it all right, but as for responding and


assisting in the development of British Columbia, they have refused.
Let me call attention to another field. I have referred to taxation and some other fields, but here is an illustration. It may seem strange that I should choose a subject such as this; I assure hon. members that I am not full of my subject. The total federal government revenue from the sale of alcoholic beverages in the year 1954-55 amounted to $176,963,000. The provincial revenue amounted to $159,873,000. I would call attention to the fact that the difference in the federal revenues was $17,090,000. Let me further state that the federal revenue includes the total identifiable taxes but does not include general sales tax on materials used in the manufacture of alcoholic beverages. The provincial revenue is for the 10 provinces and the figure includes not only the direct taxes but also receipts from permits, fines, confiscations, etc. I would suggest, Mr. Chairman, that here we have a case where the federal government received over $17 million more than the provinces did in revenue from alcoholic beverages, yet the provinces were saddled with the cost of administration. They were responsible for alcoholic research and for the rehabilitation of those who had become addicted to alcohol. They were responsible for providing housing for those who were put in prison because of this thing. The provincial governments had to assume all the responsibility, including the criticism attached to this type of business, and now the federal government comes along and takes $17 million more than does the provincial government. I cannot see any sense of justice or fairness in a situation like that. I am not speaking for the alcohol industry. So far as I am concerned, we would be better off without it. I believe that the revenues are far offset by the cost to the nation. But there is the picture. So I say, Mr. Chairman, the government is indicating a failure to properly understand and estimate the expenses the provinces have.
I know the federal government thinks their expenditures are increasing. They talk about defence and all these other things that have increased. I remind you again that according to the figures put on the record just the other day by the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke, the increase so far as the provinces and municipal authorities are concerned is far in excess of that in the federal field. Government expenditures for 1954 compared with 1955 show the increase in the federal field was 5-5 per cent; provincial, 292 per cent and municipal, 276 per cent. We see, therefore, just where the increase in costs exists. It is at the provincial and municipal levels and not so much on the federal level.

The supercilious attitude taken by this government is being resented by the provinces. I wish they would forget this attitude, "We will allow you", and get down to business and work out an agreement that would be mutually satisfactory. I can somehow smell a carryover from Bill No. 3 of last year when this government thought they had to safeguard the rights of the people of Canada and protect them against the poor judgment or perhaps the vicious schemes of the provincial authorities. I am inclined to think this is somewhat of a carryover.
I took note, Mr. Chairman, of the retort of the Minister of Finance to the statement made by the leader of this group when he referred to the proposals as niggardly. The minister said he could not understand that type of language. He could not see where it fitted into this particular type of thing. Then, he went on to refer to the increase that would accrue to the provinces from contributions under this new proposal. It is something like the children who come to the father and say, "Dad, look at our shoes. They are just in tatters; the soles are worn out; our toes are sticking out; the laces are gone and the heels are worn out. We need some new shoes." The father, even though he can see it, says, "I see that; I understand. I tell you, we will put new heels on those shoes." He thinks this should satisfy the children. I would suggest that the Minister of Finance should take a look at the thing, and this is somewhat comparable. He should look at the increase and not say, "We are going to put new heels on the shoes". Bless my soul, he ought to buy new shoes. When you think of the budgetary surplus to which the leader of our group has referred, and when you think of the surpluses that are building up, he could well afford to buy them new shoes and not just put heels on the old shoes.
The Fraser Valley Record of Wednesday. July 11, has an editorial entitled, "Time For Tax Cuts". I shall read the first sentence of the editorial:
In the first two months of this fiscal year, ended May 31, the Canadian government showed a surplus of $274 million.
Further down we find this paragraph:
There is a theoretical limit, declares the Financial Post, to this intelligent paternalism. If there were no limit, the government would be right to bag all the money and then spoon it out; and that would be the end of economic freedom.
I was going to refer to the remark of the leader of the C.C.F. party regarding natural resources. He said that some provinces were more greatly blessed than others and therefore they should be willing to share. Well, we agree in that; we believe we should share.

May I suggest that the extent of the natural resources in any given province is of great importance, but there is something of greater importance, and that is how the natural resources of a province are conserved and developed. I would suggest that every province has deposits of natural resources, but to a substantial degree it depends upon the vision, the wisdom and the initiative of the provincial administration to develop those resources or to have them developed in the interests of the people of the province.
The hon. member for Macleod referred to the Financial Post. I want to quote just one sentence from the same article to which he referred:
Government-with a new boldness of concept-
I wish the hon. member for Kamloops were here. He rather snorted when the hon. member for Macleod was reading this. I continue:
Government-with a new boldness of concept-is directing record capital outlays to push communication and transportation services into all parts of the country, to facilitate the big undertaking, bring a new degree of cohesion to the province and all that is taking place therein.
I would suggest, Mr. Chairman, that if the members of this house, the Liberals, the Conservatives, the C.C.F.'ers were as great statesmen as those who founded confederation they would cast aside their prejudices as the fathers of confederation did at that time, they would throw their political philosophies out the window, and they would join with Social Credit and march with us toward that great new era that lies before us under a Social Credit administration. I believe, Mr. Chairman, you are attempting to rise.

Mr. Chairman, I realize that in rising to speak to this resolution I am doing si m rather a dual capacity. I have the honour to represent one of the finest constituencies in Alberta, but at the same time I have been the mayor of one of the finest towns for almost 12 years. More than that, I view this resolution with some concern.
I have had some nine years' experience as a board member of one of the large school units and I know the problems that prevail there in so far as administration is concerned. I should like to say this. Never in the history of our province, to my knowledge, have we been handed a package deal which we must accept whether we like it or not. It is the responsibility of this government to sit in conference with the provincial levels of
6082	HOUSE OF
Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements administration and discuss the merits of this new tax agreement. After all, what is government but the manager of our biggest business, namely, the business of government? How does the authority become vested in this federal government ruthlessly to walk over the rights that were handed down at confederation to the leaders of the provinces? Where does the revenue come from that they are going to dole back rather niggardly to the people who earn it and who pay it out of their own pockets? Where have they the right to sit in judgment and dictate what shall be done with the revenues accruing within the provinces of this country?
We can see the tendency to centralize, as has been indicated several times. More and more the rights and the autonomy of the people of the provinces have been filched away from them and I think it would be fitting if this federal government set aside this resolution or this bill at this time and called into conference the premiers and their respective ministers and sat down and discussed this thing once again and tried to come up with at least a better solution to our over-all problem.
I know that some people say that the time element is of the essence. We have been sitting here for almost seven months. Not a bit of legislation has come up so far that is comparable with this or as far-reaching. This is a measure that is going to affect not only federal economy but provincial economy. I believe we have a very serious responsibility here to see that what the fathers of confederation fought so hard to establish shall not be ruthlessly thrown out the window. I know that we in Alberta are perhaps more privileged than many other provinces. For the last 20 years we have been blessed with a government that has a heart, a government that has vision, a government that realizes that our God-given natural resources are not there for the purpose of feathering the nest of political opportunists, but to be developed and the proceeds accruing put in trust and then handed back in terms of doing the most good for the most people, according to the best collective thinking of those charged with that responsibility. It is because of that that in a matter of 20 years our province has come from a state of bankruptcy to solvency. We were $167 million in debt. It required 51 cents of every revenue dollar to pay the interest on the debt alone. We have come from a state of bankruptcy to a state today where we have an over-all surplus of $180 million after our provincial debt is retired. It is the only province in Canada, or the only state on the North American continent, where half the revenue involved in our budget, which incidentally is $242 million, comes from
[Mr. Yuill.l

the development of our natural resources and the profits accruing from them. It only requires roughly 50 cents on every tax dollar to be raised in the accepted tax medium. We have had demonstrated time after time that our government is a government with a heart, one that has taken the responsibility of providing for its people.
Concerning the resolution that is presented here I do not think any one of us-feels there should be dual taxation; I do not think it is either desirable or necessary. But I do think that those who are charged with the sacred responsibility of administering the affairs at the provincial level should be shown the courtesy and granted the right-of sitting in conference and endeavouring with the advice and co-operation of the federal government to come up with an answer that will be the right answer.
I am afraid that if this resolution is passed it will be altogether too rigid, and I certainly hope it will not be passed. I think there should be at least some measure of flexibility so that in the future, if it is demonstrated that this is not a satisfactory or efficient agreement, the provinces will not be pushed aside when they ask for a new deal or a new look at the existing agreement. I am inclined to the belief that if and when they come they will be told, "We are hewing to the line; that is the letter of the act and consequently we cannot do anything to help you."
As I said a moment ago, Mr. Chairman, we in Alberta have come a long way in the last 20 years. We have been able to provide benefits to the people of Alberta far beyond those provided in any other province of Canada. British Columbia is fast approaching the standard established in Alberta, but of course there is a reason for that: it is because they have a Social Credit government.
As is common in all provinces, we have a need for roads, we have needs in education and needs in the field of health. I think those matters are surely a part of the responsibility of the major government. It is true that in a sense it has been contributing in some way, but basically only to health and welfare, and I think the share that is put up is not over generous.
Let us take the case of education, for example. In Alberta, when our government took over 20 years ago, the best education standard we could expect to find anywhere outside the cities and some of the towns was grade 8. The government of that day seemed to think that was the height of its responsibility. When our government took over, it definitely declared itself in favour of the equalization of educational opportunities. It decreed that any child regardless of

who he was or where he lived should not be denied anything short of a grade 12 education.
In order to make that possible it was necessary to centralize, from an educational point of view. I happened to be one of the original members of the divisional board in our part of the country at that time and I can tell you something about the position we were in then. This was back in 1939, of course, right after the hungry thirties, and the members of the teaching profession were in the worst plight they have ever experienced in all their lives. We had teachers working for as little as $300 a year. The best teachers and the principals of high schools earned the glorious salary of $750 a year.
When we took over the administration of some 105 schools we found even at that low level of pay some $20,000 was owed in back pay. In some cases we found that some teachers were owed salaries by as many as five different schools. It is recognized across the country that in Alberta today we have the highest standard of education. With the possible exception of British Columbia, the salaries of our teachers are higher than anywhere else in Canada.
In order to make grade 12 education possible to students it was found necessary to set up centralized units. It was also necessary to provide modern transportation and, further, it was deemed necessary to hire special teachers to teach such special subjects as home economics, shop, agriculture, music, art, business and many of these subjects that in some quarters are perhaps looked upon as frills but which are nevertheless within the orbit of a normal grade 12 education.
All of these things cost money, and the job of the school board was a pretty tough one, as we soon discovered. Our government realized it was necessary to give more and more assistance. In the last ten years the outright grants on a per pupil basis have jumped from $19 to approximately $120. In round figures this represents an increase in the last ten years of $100 per pupil. Naturally there has been a boon in the management of school affairs. The demand for new buildings, modern transportation and added services increased and the fact that grade 12 education was established meant that the school population increased at a rapid pace. Those who in most cases moved out following grade 8 stayed and received grade 12 education. All of these things are characteristic of all the provinces and they are not peculiar to our own community. These things posed an almost impossible problem to the administrative board.

The government has increased its assistance. Last year it provided more than $38 million for education alone. It realized that in spite of its ever-increasing generosity the problem would continue to exist and enlarge because of the increased demands through larger enrolments. The government realized this was posing a problem for the direct school taxpayer. A year ago the government pegged the school mill rate and provided $6,600,000 as a subsidy. It discovered that $7,108,000 was required to pull up the slack this year.
In the reshuffle that is apparently going to come about I think it would be possible for this government out of a budget of better than $4f billion to provide, over and above the specified terms of this formula, not less than $250 million in order to provide the provinces, irrespective of their location, with at least the minimum or the bottom of the barrel in services. Speaking strictly from the municipal point of view, I think it must be agreed that the problems are much the same wherever you go. Out of a budget of $242 million my province has seen fit to set aside $71.5 million for direct and indirect financial assistance to municipalities.
The city of Edmonton perhaps offers the best illustration of the need for quite considerable financial assistance, far beyond the ability of the province to render. Thanks to the generosity of the provincial government in the last five years Edmonton has received $40,942,541 in the way of direct and outright cash assistance. In the same period it has had the opportunity to borrow at interest rates as low as 2 per cent and not more than 3J per cent a total of $57,292,900. Out of the surpluses accruing from the development of natural resources our province has set aside a revolving fund which has made it possible for municipalities of all sizes to borrow at that low rate of interest, thereby saving over $2 million a year in interest rates alone. Believe me, a dollar saved is a dollar earned.
If this government would just hold its shot a little bit and not be too anxious to railroad this thing through, if it would just take another look and take the various leaders of the provinces into its confidence, if it would agree to talk over this thing sensibly and in the spirit of the fathers of confederation, I am sure they all would come up with a more lasting and more satisfactory answer to our problems.
I am not going to take up any more time, but I should like to say that in my little town of only 2,000 population we received direct cash assistance amounting to $14,000 which came out of the provincial gasoline tax. Half of the 10-cent tax, or 5 cents a gallon, was

Patent Act
set aside and divided across the board according to population. In that town we have sewers, natural gas, cement sidewalks and everything you could expect in a small town. Our debenture commitment is around $13,000 per year. As a consequence of this grant we were able to turn around and pay back the government in its own coin. We were able to show a substantial cash surplus and also enjoy a revenue accruing from the utility itself. There are not many cases where you can have your cake and eat it too from the municipal point of view. We have been able to reduce our tax rate by 19 mills, which does not alter the fact that in spite of that generosity we are momentarily faced with a tax rate of 48 mills.
I think it would be in the interests of humanity and everyone concerned from the federal government down to the smallest province if a more realistic view of this thing were taken. We should take another look at it and see if we cannot come up with a better and more satisfactory solution.
