speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 292, to amend the Patent Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill deals with a subject which I believe is very important to the welfare of Canada. It deals with an aspect of control over our industrial life which throughout the years has become most involved and intricate. It seems to me that it is important to the industrial future of this nation that the way in which patents have been used, in many instances to restrict competition, to restrict production and in fact to restrict the general development of the arts of production, is something which should be looked into, and for which a solution is required.
In the past patents were valuable to the nation to the extent that they created an incentive to invest and resulted in reward for invention in a fair and reasonable way. However, with growing industrialization and the increasing size of corporations, with the growth and development of international cartels, the old concepts in relation to patents are to a large extent no longer valid and it is essential that a new look be taken at this whole field.

Hon. members are aware that by order in council of June 10, 1954 the government appointed a royal commission to inquire into this general field and I am pleased that as chairman there was appointed a man of the ability and integrity of Chief Justice Ilsley. If there is any man in the nation whom I have known rather intimately and who I believe is a conscientious person, one who will do his best to see that a fair solution is obtained, it is Chief Justice Ilsley. Quite a number of members of the house had the privilege of serving in parliament when he was minister of finance or occupied other portfolios in the government. We came to respect him. We are confident that the work he is now doing in this field will be important to Canada and will add to our material welfare in the years ahead.
It is a very complicated study. When I first looked into the matter I thought that perhaps the solutions would be very obvious and that with obvious solutions the government should act immediately. I still think there are some obvious steps that should be taken but I am quite prepared to say that many eminent people have spent a lifetime studying in this field and that among the experts there is not always agreement. Therefore one may say: Why do you have the temerity to advance a private members' bill? I do so not because I say that the provisions of the bill will remedy the situation and solve all the problems. I do so because I feel there should be an increasing amount of attention and consideration given throughout the nation to this very important question.
I believe there is no more appropriate place to discuss this general field than the parliament of this nation. By introducing the bill at this time I am hoping to have the matter aired, to give it some further publicity throughout the nation and to help in a small way to bring attention to the problem in the hope that solutions will be found in the not distant future. I hope that the government will study the suggestions made here along with any other suggestions that may be brought to them from time to time. I ask the government to look at the whole problem objectively and to act in the interests of the whole Canadian nation.
Before the Ilsley commission have appeared a number of eminent witnesses. I happen to be a resident of Saskatchewan and I suppose if I am acquainted with problems discussed in a public way more in one area than in any other it would be in that province. The daily newspaper to which I subscribe is the Regina Leader-Post. That newspaper has not always agreed with me. As a matter of fact if a census were taken I suppose it would show that it usually disagrees with

me. No matter, I will say that the Regina Leader-Post and the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix, acting in this general field under the direction of the publisher, Clifford Sifton, have done and are doing an excellent public service.
I notice that they have been questioned as to the reason for their general interest in this field. They have said that they are interested not because anything that has been done has affected their business particularly but rather as newspapers who feel it is a public service to take into account the interests of their subscribers, the interests of consumers generally. Having that public spirited attitude, they obtained the services of three very eminent persons qualified in this field. Those persons made presentations to the commission and were subject to cross-examination and general discussion.
The first I shall mention is a Canadian, Ian Malcolm MacKeigan, who for many years was a public servant of this nation. In the fall of 1941 the combines organization took over the supervision of the law enforcement work of the wartime prices and trade board for the next five years, during the latter part of which Mr. MacKeigan was deputy enforcement administrator of the board. Mr. MacKeigan's special responsibility in this field was that of supervising the enforcement of food rationing, gasoline and tire rationing and related black market activities. He went from this position to the Combines Investigation Act administration and was appointed deputy commissioner. He served in that position until 1949 when he resigned. He has certainly studied this field very carefully.
The second person who appeared on behalf of the two newspapers to which I have referred was Judge Thurman W. Arnold, a noted and very competent expert in the United States. For years he was assistant attorney general in charge of the justice department's anti-trust division. He engaged in many suits in this field and became known as a rather famous trustbuster, to use a common term. He is a recognized international authority in the patent field.
The third person was Walton Hale Hamilton who has spent many years on the staffs of many prominent universities in the United States and who for a number of years was special assistant to the attorney general of the United States dealing with this general field. I believe that the knowledge they bring to this question and the evidence they have placed before the commission are valuable and I am sure will result in benefit to this nation.
We need to look at this field more today than we have in the past because the whole 67509-386
Patent Act
pattern of invention has been changing. When patent laws were first considered and enforced hundreds of years ago it was because some individual had invented some device and people thought it was fair to give him a reward for his invention. It was also thought necessary to hold out the promise of a reward in order to entice the individual to make his invention public. For these reasons the whole patent system was established. Today the role of the individual inventor, the single person who comes up with an idea and turns it into a practical device, is diminishing. There are few individuals who alone play an important part in this field. The whole general field of invention has been taken over by big industries, by the great laboratories. Giant corporations will hire many of the best brains in a certain field, place these people in a laboratory, give them an assignment, and ask them to inquire into a particular field of science in the hope that they may come up with some useful innovation.
It is important to us that we remove the restrictions that have been provided by patents not only because we need to increase the production of this nation to the fullest possible extent but for another major reason. It is being impressed upon me more and more that there is in this world a nation that, in industrial techniques is making rapid strides, sometimes frightening strides. We read statements of many high placed persons who have toured the U.S.S.R. We have been told by such a prominent person as James S. Duncan, president and general manager of the Massey-Harris Company, that in the U.S.S.R. there are being trained today from two to three times as many scientists as are being trained on this continent. He pointed out that they are using their human resources in a determined drive for ever-increasing production. In certain fields we have been hearing of late that they may be ahead of us.
We need to free inventions not only to increase production so that we ourselves in this nation may have a higher standard of living but for this other reason. I think it is imperative that we do everything that is in our power as a parliament to see that free institutions are more effective in providing an increased standard of living and increased production than any other system in the world. If we are to make certain to stay ahead-as I am certain all of us wish we can-in the production field, we must give more attention to the problem that I have been discussing.
Often in the past patents have been used not in order to add to knowledge, not to bring forward new inventions and new products, but rather to restrict the field so that those who can occupy it by the patent device

Patent Act
are able to make extremely large profits. The illustration that has been used over and over again is what happened when it became known that a sulfa drug could be useful in treating certain diseases. The main sulfa drug at the time was sulfanilamide. It was a dye. The patent covering this material had long ceased to exist. The process had reverted to the public domain. When it was discovered that sulfa could be used in the medicinal field, a certain company found a derivative which they called sulfathiazole and applied for a patent. Soon after they applied for a patent it was learned that another company was applying for a patent for the very same material. It was not a case of judging which company had the patent, either by a patent commissioner or by the courts. The two companies got together. One said, "You have better marketing facilities than we have". The other said, "You have better production facilities". So they said, "Rather than compete, we will work together to maintain prices and to assure high profits for both firms". When they looked further into the matter they found that there were other companies working along the same lines. They therefore decided that one company would obtain the patent and that then they would licence other companies which had made certain progress in this field. Finally nine companies got together and controlled the production, distribution and sale of sulfathiazole and sulfa drugs generally. In my opinion, no one can defend the use of patents in this way. No one can say that by this use the public was being benefited. As a matter of fact, the patent system or the licensing system was used for one purpose only, namely to restrict competition and to make extremely large profits for the companies involved.
A little bit earlier I said that large corporations make most of the new inventions and that for the individual there is no longer any great place in the field of invention. The experience of Sinclair Oil Company serves to substantiate this claim. The company sent out a questionnaire asking for suggestions for improvements in petroleum products that might be adopted and that it received 6,000 replies. Among the 6,000 replies, the Sinclair Oil Company found only 400 ideas of any substance. Of the 400 ideas they found only 30 to be in the general field of petroleum products. Out of the 30 they found only 3 that made any industrial sense. Of the 3, only one was capable of production, but it was uneconomical and impractical. Hence, making a general inquiry among individuals in a particular field may not be very remunerative. If invention takes place and is accomplished, it is now done by vast teams

of scientists, in modern laboratories, with adequate equipment and working together. They produce inventions.
The General Motors Corporation, which I believe is the world's largest corporation, has pointed out that the inventions so obtained are not obtained by individuals but are obtained in the General Motors research laboratories, and that once an invention is obtained in the laboratories credit is not given to a specific person or even to a number of individuals. Rather, they say that the fact is that a great number of people in the laboratories have contributed to the final invention and that the idea of remunerating the individual for an invention is obsolete since it has been brought about by a modern laboratory of a large corporation.
A large corporation can then produce the invention. It can obtain the patent. After it obtains the patent on an invention it does not say, "We will wait 17 years and after the 17-year period we will allow the invention to revert to the public domain". Oh, no. They usually say, "We will spend time, energy and money in order to dream up all sorts of variations of the invention, all sorts of tiny amendments to it, so that if anyone challenges the invention we shall have such a conglomeration of inventions in this field that we shall declare that some of them are being infringed". They go further. As a large corporation controlling a huge number of inventions, if any other company wants to use one of its inventions they say that, in obtaining a licence, it must agree that it will never at any time challenge the validity of the patent held by the patentee. This means in effect that a giant corporation can control a large area of the industrial art and that new companies coming into the field, if they know what is good for them and if they want to exist in a commercial way, will accept the facts of life by going to the company that has control of this huge number of patents, applying for a licence, paying the royalties, agreeing to its terms, and hoping thereafter to make a profit on its production.
If a smaller new company believes that the patents held by the giant company are weak and cannot be maintained in the courts, history shows that the company is probably still well advised to do nothing about its conviction, to spend no money challenging the patent, but obtain a licence and meet the conditions. A classic example often used is that of Eastman Kodak Company versus the Boston Camera Company. The Boston Camera Company needed a certain number of licences for patents. They believed that the Eastman Kodak Company was controlling very weak patents, and that in fact most of

the patents controlled by the Eastman Kodak Company would not be held valid if challenged in the courts. So, the Boston Camera Company began production on its own. The Eastman Kodak Company instituted a long series of suits against the Boston Camera Company. The Boston Camera Company won every court case, but used all its money and soon became the property of the Eastman Kodak Company. Here is an example of patents being used in a rather predatory fashion to control the whole field of the industrial art.
Another classic example of patents being abused and used for purposes against the public interest is the use Standard Oil made of its patents for butyl rubber. Butyl rubber was the forerunner of modern synthetic rubber. This company did not develop its patents but decided to restrict them and allow their use only for the production of a very expensive product. The Standard Oil Company agreed with the I. G. Farben Company that it would not develop butyl, and the I. G. Farben Company agreed to keep out of the general territory of the Standard Oil. Prominent people have come to the conclusion that the role Standard Oil played in preventing the development at an early date of synthetic rubber was very expensive and costly, and proved a menace to the very existence of democracy in the war with Germany. Here is another classical instance of patents being used as a method of restricting and preventing production.
Now, may I refer to an example a little closer to home. It has been pointed out that the Fairview Chemical Company Limited of Regina, a very small company, decided a few years ago to produce a dust treatment for the control of smut in grain and for the control of wire worm. It decided, on the work done by Dr. A. P. Arnason whom I knew personally in Saskatoon that it had arrived at a good formula for mixing the two main components going into this chemical for the treatment of smut and the prevention of wire worm damage. The two chemicals were mercury and benezene hexachloride. Mercury had been used for many years in one form or another as a fungicide to control smut and other harmful seedborne spores. Benezene hexachloride had for some time been used in the control of wireworms. This company decided that if it could mix mercury and benezene hexachloride it could obtain one substance that could be used by the farmer to control both smut and wire-worms. They decided they would go into the production of this chemical. They learned however that another company had applied for a patent. It was pointed out 67509-386J
Patent Act
that the patent was granted on a so-called invention that was just as simple as mixing flour and sugar, and because this company obtained a patent the Fairview Chemical Company Limited of Regina decided, being a small company, that it could not afford to contest the patent. Instead it would either cease to produce this chemical substance or would pay a licence fee.
It was pointed out that the patent given in this instance was very costly so far as agricultural producers were concerned. The consumer wishing to obtain the patented article had to pay $7 per pound, whereas this company could easily have sold the mixture for $5.25 per pound. On the potential market available for that year, it was estimated that agriculture producers lost $17,500. This is another example of a patent being abused.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I wish to refer to the general suggestions contained in this bill. The first one is the suggestion that the provision which now allows for free licensing of any invention used in the production of food or medicine should be extended. It should be extended not only to include the method of production but the end products themselves, namely the foods or medicines and also include other articles in the field of health such as optical goods, dental goods, dental and surgical instruments and equipment and devices such as wheel chairs and artificial limbs. I suggest that is a reasonable provision, and if it were placed in the law it would allow, consumers of many of these goods to obtain them at lower prices.
The second main suggestion is for amendments to the general abuse section in the patent act. It is suggested that the Attorney General of Canada or any person who, at any time after the expiration of three years from the date of the grant of the patent, applied to the commissioner alleging in the case of that patent that there has been abuse of the exclusive rights thereunder, could ask that a license be issued.
At the present time the interpretation is based on the word which is being deleted, the word "interested" before "person", which has been defined as a person who is in the field already and is associated with the production of those articles. A further suggestion is that not only if the demand for an article is not being adequately met can a licence be granted as of right but that this should be extended to include any potential demand so that any potential demand for a cheaper model of the same article may result in a licence for production being granted. Butyl rubber, the example I used a few moment ago, might apply here. The invention was used

Patent Act
in the production of a very expensive commodity only. This new provision would allow a licence to be granted on the ground that while the invention was being developed it was not being developed to take care of potential demand for a cheaper article.
It is further suggested that licences should be granted not on the narrow basis of the interest of the person concerned or about to be concerned in the production itself, but the provision should be extended to include considerations of the general public interest. If this were done a licence would no doubt be granted in many more additional instances.
It is further suggested that a licence should be granted when the establishment of any new trade or industry has been prejudiced so that patents may not be used to restrict the establishment of new trade and industry in this nation. A further important suggestion is that the commissioners should be given the right to issue a licence if an applicant for a licence to a patent can show that the said patent is part of a portfolio which is being used to lessen competition in the field they control.
It is further suggested that if an applicant for a licence can show that the patent is part of a portfolio substantially controlling an industry in Canada, then the commission should be given the additional power to grant a licence for the import of the article into our country. An example was the Arvin radio case. The suggestion here is that a licence could be granted if it could be shown that a portfolio is not only being used to discourage production but also to limit the field of consumption.
A further suggestion is that the owner of any substantial accumulation of patents, in either a portfolio or a pool, must register with the restrictive trade practices commission, a statement of their patents, a statement of their patent policy in enforcing them, a justification for the royalties, and so on. It is believed that if such a declaration is made public policy there will be less chance of companies using their patent system in order to prevent competition or control production.
I see that I have taken almost the whole of my allotted time, Mr. Speaker. I did not expect to take so long this afternoon. I want to conclude by saying, as I did when I began, I fully realize that this field is very complex; that over the years many experts have given a great deal of attention to it. There has been much genuine and conscientious difference of opinion as to what should be done in the national interest; but I am fully convinced that a new attack must be made on the restrictive use of patents in this country so that in the years to come production may be raised to the highest level.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with great interest to the remarks which have been made by the sponsor of this bill. The general remarks he made before getting down to explanations about the proposals themselves were indeed quite interesting, and I am sure that the Ilsley commission will be quite interested in reading those remarks which deal with the general subject itself.
The hon. gentleman also gave illustrations of some of the facts which he thinks should should be corrected in this inquiry which is now going on and which is headed by Chief Justice Ilsley. He referred to the chairman of the commission, Chief Justice Ilsley, in terms with which I think everyone in this house will agree. We know that this commission is doing an excellent job at the present time. The assistants to the Chief Justice, namely, Mr. Buchanan and Mr. Favreau, are giving considerable assistance I should also mention the fact that they are being given great help by the secretary of the commission, Mr. Laidlaw. I had occasion to meet the members of the commission to discuss some of the matters which were brought to my attention, and I may say I am fully convinced the report that they intend to bring down-and, as I indicated, this report will probably be brought down in the spring of next year-will be a report which will, I am sure, satisfy most people interested in that field. When I say that, I should also add that everybody should take interest in this matter. It is, as the hon. gentleman said, a very complex matter, in which one has to have special qualifications to be able to deal with it in a manner that may be as constructive as one would wish.
I should like to take a few minutes, if the house will allow me, to give some of the background of the legislation itself. Patents have been granted in Canada since 1824; that is, in Lower Canada, at the time, and in Upper Canada from 1826 up to the time of confederation. Shortly after confederation, that is in 1869, the first act was passed under the authority of the British North America Act, which gives full jurisdiction to the federal government in the matter of patents of invention. The Patent Act, which was passed in 1869, has often been amended but it is in its broad terms essentially the same.
The basic feature of the legislation is that it provides for the grant of an exclusive right for a limited time, 17 years in this case, to an inventor in return for the disclosing of his invention to the public. The purpose of this is to stimulate the making of inventions and the advancement of science and technology for the welfare and economic

benefit of the people of the country. It is an exclusive privilege but it is not absolute.
The statute contains certain provisions intended to ensure that the grant of such privilege-which is a definite privilege for a period of 17 years-will promote not only the making of new inventions, but also their early working on a commercial scale in Canada wherever possible.
During the life of the patent, the patentee is required to supply the public demand for the patented article in Canada to an adequate extent and on reasonable terms. At the expiration of the patent the invention becomes public property. Those provisions of the act which aim at safeguarding the interests of the public are the ones involved in the bill presented by the hon. member. In other words, the bill would tend to extend the nature of those licensing provisions that are provided for under the act.
The hon. gentleman referred to the first clause of the bill in which there is a proposal which would add to the licensing provisions in the case when they are granted immediately upon demand. We are concerned with patented inventions relating to food, and medicine, and the other articles that are mentioned in this clause including articles vital to health, such as optical goods, dental goods, dental and surgical instruments and equipment, et cetera.
As I have already said, the statute presently provides for compulsory licensing in the case of a patented chemical process for the production of food or medicine, even in the absence of any proven or alleged abuse of rights and this at any time after the issuance of the patent. In the case of any other invention, the patentee is given three years within which to start working it in Canada on a commercial scale. If at the expiration of that period of time he does not supply the public demand in Canada on reasonable terms and to a reasonable extent, the commissioner of patents may grant one or more compulsory licences to others to manufacture and sell the article in question, or even revoke the patent if no other means of relief can be found.
The hon. member said there were many such abuses and he cited examples. Nevertheless the fact remains that during a period of 35 years I am informed that only three applications for licences concerning chemical processes for the production of medicine have been granted and only about three dozen applications for licensing other patented inventions. In other words, that might indicate there may have been abuses which were not brought to the attention of the commission. The fact remains, however, that
Patent Act
during the long period of 35 years licences for the manufacture of medical articles were granted in only three cases and there were about three dozen applications for other articles. It may be that abuses have increased in number. But it remains a fact that during the long period of years I mentioned only those cases to which I referred were brought to the attention of the commission.
In connection with inventions pertaining to the field of health, the bill proposes that the compulsory licensing provisions be extended to articles vital to health, such as optical goods, dental goods, and surgical instruments. There may at first sight be much merit in that proposal. However, this whole subject is a very complex one and a proposal of this nature should not, I suggest, be adopted without careful analysis and expert advice as to all its angles and implications. The results obtained under the present provisions must be weighed against those sought to be achieved through the amendment. For instance, if generic terms are to be used together with an enumeration of specific items as illustrations of the scope and meaning of the generic terms, great care must be taken that, in the net result, some important item might not turn out to have been inadvertently excluded or omitted.
With reference to the second part of the proposals which my hon. friend made, he stated that in order to be considered as a person "interested" who can apply to the exchequer court for invalidating or voiding a patent or to the commissioner of patents for a compulsory licence under the existing provisions, one must be already in active competition with the patentee, which condition, he pointed out, often cannot be fulfilled in the case of a new product.
I submit that is not exactly the case. In fact, under the act as it now stands there is a provision under which a person who simply proposes to make, sell or use an article may apply to the court for a declaration that this will not constitute an infringement of a particular patent. In other words, he does not have to be in active competition. He simply has to declare that he intends to manufacture an article. Surely that does not mean he is in active competition at the time, and he can ask the court for a declaration that this will not constitute an infringement of a particular patent.
As to the nature and extent of the interest required to obtain a compulsory licence from the commissioner of patents, my information is that it has not been considered necessary for an applicant to be already in active competition with the patentee in order to qualify for a compulsory licence. I think that is only

Patent Act
normal. The commissioner will, however, require the applicant to show that he intends to use the patented process or to manufacture the patented article and that he has the financial means to do so. In other words, he satisfies himself that the applicant is serious and is a bona fide applicant. Otherwise anyone could challenge whoever has obtained a patent of invention and there would be no protection for the patentee.
I would like to deal now with what I consider to be the more important part of the proposals involved in the bill. These are the proposals that deal with the abuses of patent rights and compulsory licensing. Perhaps one feature of those provisions which should more particularly be looked into by the commission is the primary requirement of manufacture in Canada and the bar indirectly placed against importations.
If one reads section 67, subsection 2, paragraph (b) of the act, one may feel that these provisions, indirectly at least, contain a bar against importations into Canada of an article that is being manufactured here when there is already in Canada a holder of a patent for a similar article. I am informed that this matter is being studied very carefully and numerous representations have been made to the commission in that respect. I am convinced the commission will give this matter a very thorough study and will investigate it fully.
The suggestion has been made that lists of patents be registered in some cases with the restrictive trade practices commission by the owners of any substantial accumulation of patents, in either a portfolio or a pool. The first remark I would like to make on this subject is that there would surely have to be a definition of what is meant by the words "a portfolio or a pool" in order that there would be no misrepresentation of the meaning. I do not think my hon. friend would subscribe to the practice of preventing an individual from holding more than one patent.
As far as the supplying of that list of people holding more than one patent to the combines investigation people is concerned, the powers under the Combines Investigation Act are already wide enough for the officials of that department to have full access to the patent division. They can obtain any information they feel they need if they wish to proceed with a prosecution or investigation. I consider it would be a wasteful duplication of records if this proposal were implemented.
The Combines Investigation Act also empowers the exchequer court to make one or more orders declaring void, in whole or in part, patent agreements, arrangements or licences, prohibiting the carrying out of any
[Mr. Pinard.l
or all of their terms or provisions, directing the grant of licences under patents or revoking patents where patent rights have been used in restraint of trade or to lessen competition. In my opinion that covers the proposal that has been made in that report. In other words, the powers are already available under the Combines Investigation Act to bring about the type of investigation to which my hon. friend has referred.
I think I should at this time give the reason why I will oppose this bill if it comes to a vote. I consider the bill as being premature. My hon. friend has referred to the fact that work is now being done by a royal commission and it would appear to me

and I think he will share my views-that to legislate at this time would be an indication on our part that we have not enough confidence in the commission to allow it to proceed with its work. It is true that that work is going to take some more time before it is completed. As I said before, I have been informed that the report will be presented in the spring of next year.

The house resumed consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Harris-Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair.
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide that the Minister of Finance may pay to a province, out of the consolidated revenue fund, in respect of any fiscal year in the period commencing on the first day of April, 1957, and ending on the 31st day of March, 1962
(a)	a tax equalization payment with respect to individual and corporation income taxes and succession duties;
(b)	a provincial revenue stabilization payment with respect to such taxes; and
(c)	a tax rental payment in accordance with a tax rental agreement that may be entered into by any province as an alternative to levying such taxes on its own behalf;
and also to authorize tax collection agreements with the governments of the provinces.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to make a few remarks at this point in the resolution's progress and I assure you I shall not detain the house unreasonably. Yesterday the leader of the party to which I have the honour to belong spoke at some length and clearly enunciated the belief of all members of this group. He clearly stated that in our opinion the measure now before us is in no way adequate nor is it fair nor does it provide fair treatment with respect to the fiscal requirements which the various provincial governments have at this time if they are to discharge properly their responsibilities to the people in the respective provinces.
One could elaborate on his statements but may I just say that in Alberta this year our budget reached $242 million. This amount is required to provide social services for a population of a little more than a million
In the interests of time I intend to confine my remarks to one single aspect of the problem, namely, the economic consequences that will result if the federal government continues with its present taxation policies, and I would particularly draw to the attention of the minister the fact that in this measure and through these taxation policies we are missing the very heart of the principle of fiscal need. I refer to the fiscal need of the people themselves and the concept that while various provincial governments are indeed desperately in need of financial assistance it is the people themselves who need help most at this time.
We are discussing a measure which is designed to provide equalization payments to the respective provinces with respect to income taxes, corporation taxes and succession duties. This measure, which is the product of various conferences and negotiations as well as the attitude of the government, misses the essential point, namely, that banc to the well-being of the nation and our people is the need to restore to the people themselves their earnings in order that they can provide those things which they are unable to afford at this time and consequently turn to the various governments to provide for them. I believe that reductions in income taxes, corporation taxes and succession duties are badly needed today and could help considerably.
As I see it, the removal of the impediment to more friendly fiscal relations between the federal government and the various provincial governments lies not only in the federal government adopting a more generous attitude toward the provinces but also in policies that will help to alleviate and remove the tremendous pressure and the demands being made at the present time on the various provincial governments. I believe that the proper way to do this is to allow the people to retain more of their earnings so that they have the facilities to meet their local levies, retain their independence and provide for their stability and growth.
Today this is virtually impossible by reason of our taxation laws under which the
6092	HOUSE OF
Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements federal government makes it impossible for people to save or to pay cash for the things they require in their everyday life. This has resulted in the inability of small businesses to borrow and municipalities to provide services. Let us examine some of the actual evidence. There are many signs indicating that there are sags in our economy which belie the claim of a booming prosperity and in many instances could well mean the beginning of a recession.
What about instalment buying in our country? This has reached the highest peak in the history of the nation. In an article appearing in the Ottawa Citizen of May 23, 1956 we have information which shows that the bills that the people of Canada owe total $2,193 million. The article goes on to say:
The amount of money Canadians owe for the things they buy on time rose to a new high of $2,193 million at the end of 1955. This was an increase of $134,900,000 in the last three months of 1955 and a rise of $327 million over the year, one of the largest increases in the post-war era, a quarterly Bank of Canada survey showed today. With the steady 1955 rise, the consumer credit bill had more than doubled over a four year period, increasing from $973 million at the end of 1951.
At the end of 1955, unpaid bills in charge accounts had increased to $376 million from $330 million at the end of September and $363 million at the end of 1954. Total instalment credit had risen to $987 million from $942 million in September and $822 million in the previous year, while personal loans had swelled to $830 million from $779 million in September and $661 million in 1954.
The significance of these figures, Mr. Chairman, strikes home when compared with the total amount of income tax collected by the federal government during the fiscal year 1954-55 for all of the provinces of Canada, namely, $2,412,197,266.67. The significance of the large amount of personal borrowings and instalment credit lies in the fact that it is nearly equal to half of the yearly budget of the government. If this instalment debt were to be paid off in one year then on the basis of the disposable income of the Canadian people for the year 1955 it would require practically 12 per cent of that amount. Quite obviously we must give the people the right to keep more of their earnings and a reduction in income taxes would help considerably.
What about the people's personal savings? In the year 1939 personal disposable income of the Canadian people totalled $4,208 million of which 7-2 per cent was savings. In 1943 it totalled $7,478 million with 23-4 per cent being savings. In 1944 it totalled $8,164 million. In that year savings were 24 [DOT] 2 per cent. It is evident that there has been a steady decline in the annual rate of savings. Let us look at the last three years. In 1953, with disposable income of $16,725 million, only 9-6 per cent was savings. In the year 1954


disposable income reached $16,747 million with 6-4 per cent being savings. During the year 1955, which incidentally was the most prosperous year in the history of Canada, the estimated disposable income was $18,285 million and the people of Canada were only able to save 8 [DOT] 1 per cent.
The telling point is the extreme drop from the year 1944 comparing it with the peak year of prosperity, 1955. I submit that a choice has to be made whether to continue with the centralizing of power vested in the federal government or to restore quite rightly some of that power over the purse to the people of Canada. Finally, I should like to say this and I say it in good faith. I venture to suggest to the Minister of Finance that the foundation for the well-being of the people of Canada and the confidence which the people of Canada have in our free way of life and in our economic system is less firmly established in the measure now before us than it would be if the Minister of Finance were courageous and bold enough to review the entire situation, overhaul the entire tax structure of this country with a view to simplification and to removing all those taxes that are crippling to the people's savings or ability to pay cash for the things they need and in the case of small businesses, to restore to them the power to acquire credit at reasonable rates of interest. I believe that is one reform that is most necessary. In doing that I believe that the Minister of Finance would not only do a good stroke of business and increase the volume of revenue required for government expenditure but at the same time would earn the gratitude of the people of Canada and the co-operation, I am sure, of every member of this house.

Mr. Chairman, this afternoon in a talk which I delivered I indicated the reasons for supposing that the Bank of Canada was forced on Canada by alien influences operating from the city of London. I suggested that the main reason the Bank of Canada was forced upon Canada was that the powers in London desired to take away from Canada the finance act of 1923.
The important element in the finance act of 1923 was that under that act the Minister of Finance could create money and spend it into circulation or lend it into circulation or otherwise use it as he felt the economy of Canada demanded, just as the Minister of Finance under the finance act of 1914 in the year 1917 printed and spent into circulation $50 million in buying Canadian goods and sent those goods over to Great Britain as a loan; and just as in that same year he created 26 million other dollars and spent them into circulation for the conduct of the war.

There are people who still persist in saying that action of that sort means that it will cause inflation. The whole secret is this: what is the definition of inflation? Inflation is a rise in prices which results from a scarcity of goods in relation to the amount of money in circulation. Consequently if money is created by the Minister of Finance and spent into circulation in such a way that it does not cause a rise in prices because of a shortage of goods, then that created money will not cause any inflation or any other undesirable condition in the economy. It was of that power that the city of London wished to deprive Canada. Why? Because that power is the power that makes the nation financially free. The minister has been sitting here and listening patiently to a great deal of talk about reducing taxes and that sort of thing. The minister himself knows, as does every person in this house, that if he taxes this nation to the very limit of its endurance he still is not able to get enough money to satisfy the needs of the various provinces in this dominion.
What is to be done about the matter? Are we to go on depending entirely on taxation, or are we going to go back and take the power the minister had under the finance acts of 1914 and 1923 and employ that power as a means of supplementing the money which is in circulation in the country, thereby enabling the people as a whole throughout the dominion to buy the goods which the dominion is able to produce and thereby raise the standard of living in less fortunate areas without deducting from the standard of living obtaining in the other provinces?
It must be quite obvious that it is not fair to Ontario or to Quebec, each of which requires all the money which they can collect within their own boundaries, if money is taken away from them to be distributed in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Newfoundland, no matter how much the people of Ontario and Quebec may desire to help those other provinces. But if the money could be created, based on the goods and services which those two central provinces can produce, and then that money distributed in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland, that would enable those provinces to buy the goods from Ontario and Quebec and would in no way detract from the amount of purchasing power or revenue available in Ontario and Quebec. Without that device, I submit that it would be impossible for us to finance the affairs of this nation in a way satisfactory and fair to the people throughout this country.
What about the dividend?

The dividend is possible. The dividend can be paid by the same means.

Why not pay it?
You fellows recognized the principle in your family allowances.

Just as soon as I am finished I should love to have questions from my hon. friend. But the simple fact that I am laying down is this. It is going to be absolutely impossible to enable the people generally throughout the Dominion of Canada to enjoy the high standard of living which the productive capacity of the Dominion of Canada would justify unless we adopt the principle which was written into the finance act of 1914 and into the finance act of 1923. We saw the performance throughout world war I. We have no excuse whatever for disregarding that performance.
I submit that the whole purpose of the financial interests in London in putting the Bank of Canada into this country was to deprive us of the finance act of 1923 which meant freedom financially.
Did the same city of London influence, motivate and dictate in relation to the Sirois commission? I promise to have something to say about that matter in this talk.
What was the nature and what were the recommendations of the Rowell-Sirois report? Over all, there are several essential recommendations, of which I am going to mention two which are, in my opinion, quite undesirable. The first one was that the provinces were to vacate personal income tax, corporation income tax, and succession duties fields. This procedure removes from a province most of its capacity for improving itself economically by developing industry which the province could otherwise do to raise its standard of living. Suppose we go on with the proposals which are now being used. Of what advantage is it to a province like Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia or any other province to expend great effort in developing industry within that province, if the more industry they develop the more they are taxed and the more money is taken away from them to go into the hands of other provinces? How can they get ahead? How are they motivated? There is the main difficulty when we suggest that the power to tax in those three fields of taxation shall be taken away completely from the provinces.
Another very important recommendation was that the dominion was to assume and carry provincial debts and to set up a finance commission to see to it that the provinces did not go into debt any further. It may be said that it is sound to put a limit on the amount that a provincial government can borrow but-

May I ask the hon. member a question?

Just as soon as I am finished my hon. friend may ask questions and I will answer him during all the time remaining this evening. But I would ask him please not to interfere with me while I am talking. I say that not because I cannot answer his questions; answering his questions is just child's play to me.
He might ask a sensible one for a change.

The point I was making is this. If we are to enable a province to build itself up or if we are to encourage it to build itself up to become great and strong and a real advantage to the nation, we must give it every advantage from the industry which it develops within the province.
May I now summarize and quote certain passages from an article by A. W. Roebuck, who now is a member of the other place, in the Labour Review. It is an address delivered in Toronto, January 3, 1941, and entitled "The Other Side of the Rowell-Sirois Report". I summarize this article in order to show what this eminent gentleman thought concerning the Sirois commission matter back there in those days while it was in the heat of discussion.
Who was A. W. Roebuck? In order that we can evaluate his judgment, I read from the Canadian Parliamentary Guide of 1951 a passage which is quite enlightening regarding the standing of this gentleman:
A barrister, K.C., and bencher Law Society. Member of Granite, Thornhill golf clubs.
Life member of Toronto Liberal association. Was candidate for Ontario legislature at general elections 1911 and 1914; for the House of Commons in 1917. Elected to Ontario legislature at general election 1934. Sworn as attorney general, minister of labour and member of hydro-electric power commission, 1934.
Now, this man had quite a lot of experience, and beyond any question his words are worth listening to.
Resigned portfolio, 1937. Re-elected at general election 1937. Resigned from the Ontario legislative assembly to be candidate for House of Commons. Elected to House of Commons at general election 1940. Summoned to the Senate of Canada, April 18, 1945. Party politics, Liberal. Religion, Anglican.
Now, this indicates we are not listening to just any idle talker when we listen to this man's speech. May I just summarize the article which was printed, as I have said, in the Labour Review? I am going to give the headings, and then there are two or three passages from which I should like to quote. The headings in this article, "The other side of the Rowell-Sirois Report" are as follows: First, "Confederation, a defence measure";

second, "Division of powers"; third, "Unity with diversity"; fourth, "The commission's work"; fifth, "Changes since 1867"; sixth, "B.N.A. Act has not held us back". And consequently there is no reason to change the B.N.A. Act or abolish it; seventh, "The Sirois Proposals"; then I propose to read from that division so that members may get this man's view of what the Sirois report proposed:
The Sirois report is a monumental document, but you will find its main recommendation stated with reasonable conciseness as follows:
(a)	The dominion government is to become solely responsible for direct relief to unemployed employables, all other relief and public charities to be borne without dominion aid by the provinces and municipalities, with the exception only of old age pensions to which the dominion will continue to contribute 75 per cent as now.
(b)	The dominion is to assume and pay the principal and interest of all the provincial debts (including both direct obligations and those guaranteed by provinces), the dominion to have the benefit of all interest collected by each province on its investments, a single exception being made of the province of Quebec where the dominion will assume 40 per cent of both provincial and municipal debts.
(c)	In return the provinces and the municipalities are to hand over all personal income taxes, corporation taxes and succession duties to the exclusive taxing power of the dominion, with the exception that a portion of the corporation tax collected from mining and oil producing companies (10 per cent is suggested) is to be returned to the provinces in which the mine or oil well is located.
(d) The subsidies guaranteed by the British North America Act from the dominion to the provinces amounting to $21,000,000 are to be cancelled.
(e)	The dominion is to pay to some provinces which are alleged to be in need an irreducible aggregate amount of $14,900,000 per annum in what are to be known as adjustment grants, to be supplemented to all provinces by emergency grants when necessity can be shown to the satisfaction of a dominion board to be appointed.
Such are the recommendations, simplified to the extent of my ability, and raising, as you may suppose an infinite series of questions.
Now, continuing with the divisions: division No. eight is, "Unemployment relief a diminishing factor;" No. nine, "Rescuing shipwrecked bondholders",-which may indicate one reason for the Sirois report; No. 10, "Centralizing financial power"; No. 11, "Poor bargain for provinces"; division 12, "Hurtful tax changes"; division 13, "Arbitrary handouts". Now, from this division, "Arbitrary handouts", may I read one paragraph?
The difficulty of determining degrees of need is obvious but the Sirois commission, whose chairman was from Quebec and upon which there was no Ontario representative, has discovered a method of calculation which to them seems satisfactory, for the commission recommends to Quebec a permanent annual grant irreducible in amount of $8,000,000 (page 96, Book II) and to Ontario the sum of nothing (page 97, Book II), and this notwithstanding that Ontario loses its confederation subsidy of $2,941,000. The grants are supposed to be made on basis of need and yet Alberta and British Columbia also lose their subsidies and get

nothing. Quebec with its irreducible grant of $8,000,000 per annum apparently has $1,100,000 greater need than all the rest of the provinces of Canada put together.
Continuing with the divisions, division 14 is, "Summing up". I should like to read the last section of 14:
(e) Recommendations which tend to destroy the basis of confederation by curtailing the sovereign power of the provinces in the management of their local affairs or placing them in financial leading strings to the dominion should be rejected.
The last division, No. 15, is "Canada has done well". May I read this one:
Political leaders may confer, newspapers pronounce, and interested parties continue their propaganda, but nevertheless public opinion will decide whether or not Canada is to be melted down and recast in some new mould; whether the Sirois commissioners are to be "Fathers of Modern Confederation" or whether their report shall be buried like many another of its kind and forgotten. We have had some most unhappy experiences of late of nations changing constitutions over night, especially so in those instances where the changes involved a concentration of power. Canada has done well and been happy in the very wide distribution which she has enjoyed in governmental authority. Let us keep it that way.
To these words I enthusiastically say, "Amen". I should like, however, to go back a little farther than we are at the present time before I say that. Obviously, from this and from other considerations, Canada had done well, and done well without the Bank of Canada. This is important.
I was arguing this afternoon as to what good the Bank of Canada has been. I believe I can challenge anyone in this house or in this country to cite one single, solitary instance in which the Bank of Canada has been of benefit, or to cite one benefit that was not enjoyed by the Dominion of Canada before the depression set in in 1929.
Evidently Canada got along very well without the Rowell-Sirois report. It was argued that the Rowell-Sirois recommendations were necessary as a war measure. Evidently from what I have already said during this afternoon, Prime Minister King did not think so. May I refer to the passage from the editorial which I quoted this afternoon from the Western Producer of January 23, 1941. These are the words:
Mr. King himself admitted that he personally was not in favour of calling the conference at this time but that he changed his mind as the result of the representations of the financial advisers of the government as conveyed to him by Mr. Ilsley.
Who were those financial advisers and how closely were they attending to what was being whispered over across the water in the city of London?
Apparently Mr. Ilsley himself had not thought Canada's war effort required the

Mr. Motherwell did not think so. The Hon. A. W. Roebuck did not think so. The Right Hon. Sir Thomas White and Beaudry Leman would not have thought so. All Canada needed to fight world war II successfully was a re-enacted Finance Act of 1923 under the Dominion Notes Act of 1868; and Canada's Bank Act in force as it was before the Bank of Canada Act modified it.
There is one matter which I think will be quite interesting to the Liberals in the house. That is the opinion of Premier Hepburn at the time when he resisted so violently and determinedly the proposals of the Rowell-Sirois commission. The opinion which Premier Hepburn held is recorded in the Western Producer of January 23, 1941. We find the article is entitled, "Hepburn Urges Money Reform; Urges Action to take Care of Expanding War Effort". The article reads:
At Toronto last weekend, following an Ontario cabinet meeting, premier Mitchell Hepburn issued a 700 word statement urging the dominion government "to make available sufficient new currency in order to take care of the expanding requirements of wartime."
He warned that a serious crisis was fast approaching and said "Canadians will look to the Bank of Canada, which must not be operated for gain or to serve selfish interests but should rather aid primary producers and which should assist in the solution of the financial problems of the provinces and municipalities of the nation.
I presume through granting loans. I go on with the news item report of Mr. Mitchell Hepburn's statement:
The statement said: "My first proposition is that the authority for creating money now vested by the constitution in the dominion government should not be delegated to any authority, public or private.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I think I have said what I had intended to say on this occasion in the various debates on this measure. It will help us greatly when we see what kind of bill the minister has to follow this resolution; but I feel that up to the present time the things which I have said were things which the nation and parliament need very much to know.
As I said this afternoon, some of these things are hidden away in remote places. Most of them have been destroyed, things which gave us an idea of how our fathers felt about the situation when the Rowell-Sirois commission was set up, was functioning and was making its recommendations and the premiers of the provinces in 1941 were deciding what they would do about those recommendations.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to take very long to sum up the position which

Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements we take on this whole matter. I think this has been a good debate, but it has not been anything more than could be expected or ought to have been expected by the House of Commons or its committees on a measure as important as this one. We look upon it as a very important measure, one that affects the provinces, the municipalities and the Dominion of Canada, not only this year but for a good many years ahead. We believe that the purpose of the debate has been served quite well. It seems to me that enough has been said at this stage to bring home to the government the feelings of the members of the house as well as the feelings of many of the governments of the provinces. We do not intend, therefore, to carry the debate any further at this stage. The resolution ought to pass and the bill be introduced so that we can have a look at it. We will take a look at the bill, Mr. Chairman, and decide what is best to do in the light of the terms and the provisions that are set out in that bill.
We thought we might influence the Minister of Finance and his colleagues to try once more to gather the provinces together in a conference with the object of working out a formula that would be more acceptable to them in the light of all of the conditions, as I said yesterday. We had no thought or desire to try to destroy the chances of getting this measure through. Frankly, we feel that the government is trying to reach some sort of solution of the financial difficulties that have arisen throughout Canada as between the provinces and the dominion and frankly between various areas of the country and the federal government. We give them credit for having made a try, and I wish to tell the minister that we look upon this tax-sharing proposal as being superior in many ways to the tax-rental scheme that has been in effect for the past ten years. I think that this proposal will mean a better deal for most of the provinces, although I must say there are some of them that will find a very slim improvement. I could name some of those, but I do not need to. The minister knows them quite well. To others, this is going to mean a considerable improvement, and I am very happy when I see what change it will make in the maritime provinces in the stabilization of their revenue. There is not any question about that, and we all rejoice in that because they have not had a decent deal. We all recognize it. They have not had their proper share of industrialization, and if they do not have some sort of balance between industrial and agricultural activity I do not see how in the world their standard of living can ever
[Mr. Low.f

be brought up to anything like the level it has reached in other parts of Canada.
So far so good; but there is still evidence that the people of the maritime provinces are not at all happy, and the best evidence that one can cite, of course, is the conference that was held in Fredericton the other day when a permanent organization was set up for the purpose of attempting to get a better deal for the maritimes. We all sympathize with them and mind you, Mr. Chairman, there are others of us who have been in a similar position in times past. I can remember when our own province was the poor relation. It is spoken of today as the Cinderella province, having come out of the kitchen and the ashes and is now dressed in slippers and beautiful evening dress. It is quite true, but that was not so long ago. We suffered the same things essentially that the maritimes suffer, but we did get a break and we have brought ourselves up through some good luck, of course, but some very good management, through the development of our resources. But some of those opportunities the maritimes have not had, and they deserve them, and every effort ought to be made to see that they do get them. I only cite these things to show that one of the purposes behind our debate thus far has been to impress upon the government the need of pausing for just a little while, thinking over the situation and giving proper weight to the conditions of the provinces and the municipalities throughout this country.
I think, without exception, the provinces find themselves unable to cope with the needs and the demands for service and for development and so on in the municipalities. And so, I thought we might be able to get the minister to call a conference once again and to make that final effort which I still think ought to have been made. I believe he is a reasonable man, and I believe that he could persuade the provinces to go along with him if he would get them together and show them that he is anxious to help them to meet their problems and to try to solve them more or less on a permanent basis. I agree with him in what he said yesterday that you cannot sit down now and draft up any scheme or proposal for tax-sharing that will stand for, well, anything more than a few years. We realize that, but I still believe that what I said yesterday is true, that he failed in drafting up the proposals he now places before the provinces to give the proper weight to the circumstances under which the municipalities and the provinces are trying to carry on.
I cannot help feeling that there should have been that one last effort to meet the

provinces, to look the facts in the face and try to carry them along with him, which he could have done. We feel perfectly satisfied on that. How much happier he would have been if he could have felt that what he proposed to the provinces would have been accepted wholeheartedly and in good spirit, and I am sure they would have gone with him.
I remind the minister that back in 1940 and 1941 when the government first negotiated the tax transfer arrangements the provinces recognized the case that was put up to them by this government. They recognized the force and the logic behind their claim that during wartime there should not be double taxation, the confusion attendant on so many different tax agencies trying to get revenues from the people, and they quite readily agreed that this government must have the wherewithal to put on a real war effort. They went along with the minister then and I am sure they would be just as reasonable now if they felt that the minister and his colleagues in the government had given sufficient consideration to the problems of the municipalities and the provinces and their circumstances. T-hey do not, and that is their unhappiness today. That is why they feel the way I said yesterday they felt.
I hope we have at least impressed upon the minister the effect on the municipal and provincial situation. We think that when he drafted the proposal that is now before us he should have taken more fully into consideration what the municipalities and the provinces will have to carry in the future. I must say to him that he could very well have lifted some of the nightmares from the provincial and municipal authorities as they look ahead into the future and see little or no hope for a solution to their terrible problems of taxation, revenues and stabilization.
You know, Mr. Minister, there are a lot of municipalities today which are saying to themselves, "I wonder what kind of burden this is going to place on us when the federal government announces its national health scheme". I am satisfied that they are going to say to themselves, "Whatever is done by the federal government, the provinces are going to try to shift a share of that on the municipalities and how are we going to meet it with the slender resources we have?" That is the thing they are thinking about extremely seriously today.
It seems to me that here was a very good chance to do something of a more or less permanent nature to help both the local governments to find a solution to their problems.
It is true that the plan we are about to consider in the bill that will be introduced does

I said yesterday that the proposal was niggardly and my hon. friend the minister contended that I was rather harsh when I said that. Let me explain, Mr. Chairman, that any new proposal is niggardly if it fails to do what is possible to be done.

possible and desirable should be made financially possible. You are becoming a good Social Crediter over there.
Those were not my words.

It will sink in after a while if we keep on. There is no question about it and I think the minister realizes that is so. I am not digressing at the moment from the thing I wanted to tell the minister. I said that any attempt to solve the problem that faces the local governments today has to be considered as niggardly if it fails to do what it is possible for us to do.
I am just as certain as I am that I stand here that if the minister had called the provinces together, even if it meant an increase of $100 million or $150 million or $200 million a year to carry them along with him in a happy mood, and had given them some hope that they could help their municipalities to solve their problems, it would have been a splendid investment and would have been possible. The minister himself knows that it would be possible. He knows full well that any time a proposal of that kind is made to help the provinces and the municipalities they are going to spend that money in development and the minute the development starts to occur taxes roll into this government, the gross national product increases and the minister's tax base is broadened. He knows that.
I want to know where the minister's faith is. He is a man of faith but it seems to me that his faith has been weak this last while. When he looks to the years ahead he must realize that his gross national product is going to continue rising and he will have a much better chance of meeting the needs of the provinces and the municipalities as well as his own needs for defence and all the other things that are demanded of him provided we get the development; but we

cannot get that development unless the municipalities and the provinces are prepared to go along and unless they have the wherewithal with which to go along. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I think we have missed an opportunity.
I had thought that the minister would yield and perhaps say, "We will hold this over; we will call a conference and after the conference has reached a decision we will bring in the legislation." That would have been much better and everyone would have been much happier about it. Those are the reasons we feel the debate has been worth while. We tried to drive these things home to the minister.
While I was speaking yesterday I mentioned something about the various problems the municipalities and provinces have. One matter I did mention briefly was that the province of Ontario as well as others faces the problem of cleaning up its rivers. Water pollution has gone so far that it is going to cost the province an estimated $120 million a year for the next 10 or 15 years. I said $120 million a year yesterday but evidently Hansard did not catch the phrase "a year" and just recorded "$120 million during the next 10 or 15 years".
