Just a few nights ago, I was looking at a television broadcast which compared the cost of living in Canada in 1936 with that in 1956, as well as comparing some other events. It brought home very vividly the tremendous difference in the amount of money that is required to give even a minimum of living standards.
Now, whether it is possible to deal with this subject within the framework of the bill now before us, at least it does seem to me it would be appropriate at the time when we are dealing with the public service superannuation that we should have a statement that there will be at this session something done to rectify an injustice which has continued far too long. We are not making any suggestion that is unrelated to reality. We are not making any rash proposals. As has been indicated, already in the United Kingdom there have been several progressive changes in the superannuation payments to a wide list of those who depend upon the government of the United Kingdom for their pensions. The last of those was during the spring of the present year. At that time it was pointed out that this is something that cannot be measured on a contractual basis. It was pointed out, as it has been pointed out on other occasions, that the civil servants, members of the armed forces and others, who received payments of that kind, accepted and received for many years payments which were far below the level of payments for corresponding activities in private occupations.
I must say that there has been a satisfactory improvement in the situation within the civil service here and in the provincial governments of Canada in recent years. Undoubtedly the gap between the amount received by civil servants and those doing similar work outside has been narrowed. We must recognize that the gap was very great indeed in earlier years. Pension payments were related to the amount they had received. Nevertheless, they were supposed to provide a minimum decent standard of living for those who were superannuated. I submit that this cannot be dealt with on a contractual basis


like an insurance policy, or something of that kind. The test is a very simple one. Do the payments they now receive provide an adequate amount to give a decent minimum standard of living to those who served their country well in those various services? An attempt has been made to meet this situation upon that basis in the United Kingdom and in the United States. They have dealt with it on more than one occasion.
It must be common knowledge to every hon. member in this house that there are many splendid citizens of advanced years who served this country, either in the civil service, the armed services or the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, who are living in really desperate circumstances because of the inadequacy of the pension they receive.
If no other jurisdiction similar to ours had dealt with this subject, then it perhaps might be argued that this is one of those unfortunate instances where a contract has been made and that the contract must stand. However, in the United Kingdom, in other nations of the commonwealth as well as in the United States a real attempt has been made to meet this situation in a spirit of justice and humanity. I do not think it is possible to put into words the anguish of many of the people who are trying to eke out an existence on the pitifully small pensions that were fixed many years ago. I do not intend to put them on record, but I have received many letters, as I am sure other hon. members have, that tell the heartbreaking story of the struggle merely to survive with the amount of the payments they receive.
I would hope that since we are dealing with civil service superannuation, and since I am sure there will be general approval of such a plan, the minister will state now that steps will be taken to provide an over-all increase in the amount of pension. That could be done immediately. Then, more elaborate procedure could be followed to examine this subject thoroughly, as it has been examined in the United Kingdom, in the United States and elsewhere, and basing the adjustments upon the time at which the payments were made and upon the very real need of those people who have given great service to Canada, this situation could be dealt with in a way that I am sure would meet with general satisfaction. I find it difficult to believe that there would be opposition from anyone if such a proposal were made.
I hope the minister, even at this stage of the session, will make an announcement that justice to those superannuated civil servants, members of the armed forces and members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police will

be meted out at this session. In that way, hope, encouragement and some faith in their prospects for the future will be given to many deserving people who are in desperate circumstances today.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION, MAKE CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that this is an appropriate occasion-and I gathered from what he said a moment ago that he intends to do it-for the Minister of Finance to make the statement which he promised on February 21 of this year he would make regarding this question. I refer in particular to the plight of superannuated civil servants, namely, those already retired who are on pensions in the lower brackets.
The fact that we are saying very little about what is in the bill that is now before us is a recognition of the fact that the steps proposed by this bill seem all to be good. As far as I can ascertain from my study of the bill, they are all steps in the right direction. They meet problems that have arisen in the administration of the Public Service Superannuation Act. Our complaint, however, is that once again the government is dealing with superannuation matters so far as our civil servants are concerned without touching this problem that faces so many of our older employees who are already retired and are having to exist on very small pensions.
I shall not take the time of the house to repeat the material in the speech that I made on February 21 of this year, as found in Hansard on pages 1415 to 1420. Neither will I attempt even to summarize the many speeches that I have been making on this subject during the regime not only of the present Minister of Finance but also of at least two of his predecessors, namely Mr. Abbott and Mr. Ilsley. I mention that fact simply to underline the situation with which we are confronted, namely, that for a long time some of us have been pleading for a measure of justice for our retired civil servants. Perhaps I might take just a moment to point out that the figures that have been given this year, as may be found on page 785 of Hansard for February 1, 1956, show that there are 2,710 retired civil servants whose pensions are less than $50 a month. That figure is included in a total number of retired civil servants of 13,022. On that same page it will also be seen that there are 4,196 widows of retired civil servants on pensions of less than $50 a month. That figure of 4,196 represents almost two-thirds of the widows of retired civil servants who are on pension. The total number of such widows is 6,459.
It is on behalf of all retired civil servants who find their pensions inadequate as the
17, 1956
Public Service Superannuation Act cost of living goes up that we plead with the minister, but we plead in particular on behalf of these folks in these lower pension brackets. As has been pointed out to the minister from this side of the house time and time again, we are not asking the government to break new ground when we ask that something be done for persons already retired, despite the argument the government continually throws at us about contractual relationships.
The Leader of the Opposition has just mentioned, as indeed I have put it on the record time and time again, that this has been dealt with by the government of the United States and by the government of the United Kingdom. It has been dealt with by the governments of a number of the states of the American union; it has been dealt with by two or three provinces of this country; it has been dealt with by private organizations like the Canadian Pacific Railway and International Nickel. In the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway the supplement which is given to certain pensioners is, I admit, cut off at age 70 when old age security comes into effect, and there are other complaints in that connection which we have already registered. But the fact is that quite a number of employers and jurisdictions have recognized that they have a moral responsibility to their former employees with respect to their standard of living after their days of active service to their employers are over.
We have made the argument time and again, and I refer to it again tonight, that the rise in the cost of living is something that has to be faced by these people and we feel a greater responsibility in this regard rests upon the government than on private employers because the government has some control over the economy of the country and some control over the cost of living.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that not only does the government owe consideration to these people because the cost of living has gone up and because they cannot get by on their small pensions but I submit also that the time has come for the government to recognize with respect to its own retired employees that people who have served their day and generation and are living in retirement have a moral right to share in the improved conditions that are achieved even after they retire.
I am sure it is not inappropriate to draw a parallel between this situation and what one would do in any ordinary decent family. I am sure any family that had its parents living in the family home and was able to improve its standard of living, if the time came when the old folks were no longer working the younger members of the family

in asking the government to do that we are asking them to do only what other governments, other jurisdictions and in many instances other employers have done already.
In addition to that I invite the government to give serious consideration to the principle or the philosophy suggested in the bulletin by William M. Mercer Limited, which I read, namely that a pension fund must be a means not just of storing up dollars based on one's past earnings but rather a means of providing employees with an equity in the future productive capacity of Canada.
Just to underline still further my contention that what we plead for is not only humanitarian, although surely that should be sufficient, but is also something to which people are giving thought in academic terms may I remind the minister of something that he probably knows, namely that this matter is being studied by experts in the professional institute which represents employees in the public service of Canada.
I have before me a very interesting article on this subject which makes a number of suggestions. The article is academic in nature and in my view is particularly well done, but because it is academic perhaps I can sum it up and give some of its suggestions to the minister just to indicate what some other people have thought about this problem and the solutions they offer. For example, it is suggested that one way to deal with the plight of superannuated civil servants whose pensions are inadequate is to supplement those pensions out of general revenue. So far as the immediate situation is concerned I think that is the only answer, but that is not a permanent answer because to do that today is to admit that 10 years from now it is going to have to be done again. In other words, the act is not completely satisfactory.
Another way to deal with this matter would be to put actuaries to work-this is suggested in the article to which I have made reference-to compute what is likely to be the rise in the cost of living, the rise in the standard of living and the rise in the productive capacity of Canada year by year during the years that lie ahead. It is difficult perhaps to be a prophet in this field, but actuaries have been able to achieve some rather accurate predictions with their research and study. It is suggested that it probably could be ascertained what additional premium or payment into the fund would be necessary by civil servants so as to provide an automatic increase in the pension after retirement of, shall we say, 2 per cent per year or whatever figure might
17. 1956
Public Service Superannuation Act be arrived at to compensate for the increased cost of living, on the one hand, and on the other hand to give to retired civil servants their share of the increased productive capacity of Canada.
That is one way it could be done and I suggest that it merits active consideration by the government. An amendment could be made to the act to provide for a slightly higher payment into the fund the purpose of which would be to guarantee to civil servants on retirement that although their pension at retirement would be at the figure arrived at by the computation set out in the act, it would go up by a fixed percentage each year from then on so that they would not have to worry about losing out in the scramble created by an increasing cost of living.
Another way, and this also has been suggested, in which this could be dealt with is by arranging for a special fund separate from the normal fund provided for by the Public Service Superannuation Act, and patterned something after the way in which supplementary unemployment insurance benefits were first brought in. I remind the minister and the government that when it was first decided to have unemployment insurance benefits of a supplementary nature for seasonal unemployment it was decided that there would be a slight extra contribution to provide for those supplementary benefits.
Similarly I suggest that it would be feasible to have a fund into which the working civil servants would contribute a small additional amount to make possible supplementary payments to those now retired. The return or quid pro quo to those now working for making that payment would be the knowledge that when they reached retirement the civil servants of that day would pay into a fund to provide whatever supplement was necessary for them. In that way our retired civil servants would continue to get their share of the increased productivity of the nation just the same as we contend that those working at any one time are entitled to an increasing share of the country's increasing productivity.
There is another suggestion which could be made in connection with this matter but which perhaps is a little more difficult to work out in connection with a government scheme. Investments might be made of certain kinds with regard to these funds so that the amount of money in the fund would reflect the increased earnings of the country at any time.

Public Service Superannuation Act
I could go into further details of these various plans but I need not do so because I think I have made my point that thought has been given to this, not just in terms of a humanitarian approach, although that should be sufficient, but also in terms of an academic approach. There are people who are studying this question because they realize the difficulties that exist. Although the government may think that the Public Service Superannuation Act is perfect, it has one sharp deficiency which is felt by hundreds or indeed by thousands of people right now and which will be felt by thousands more in the years that lie ahead.
Therefore it does seem to me that the statement which on February 21 the minister promised to make is one that should be made in the light of its importance. I hope he will arrange the business of the house tomorrow so that this can be dealt with without having another break. This matter has been interrupted time and time again during the session and I hope arrangements can be made so that he can deal with it in the morning and let the house know that the government is at last becoming aware of the seriousness of this problem, is at last becoming aware of the fact that something has to be done about it. I hope that the minister in his statement will not just repeat the negative answers which Mr. Ilsley and Mr. Abbott gave, but rather that he will indicate that the government knows that the time has come to do something about his problem.
I do no know just what the plans are for the moment, so I suppose I had better play
safe and move the adjournment of the debate.
